He can confess the shame to a friend instead of exploding at his wife. He can address the actual cause instead of ventilating the symptom onto whoever is nearest.

What anger does to the ones who receive it

I have written mostly about what a man's anger is and where it comes from, but I have to say a word about what it does, because understanding the mechanics of anger can become a way of excusing its damage, and I refuse to let that happen. A man's anger, whatever its hidden source, lands on real people, and it does real harm, and no amount of insight into its origins changes what it does to a child who lives in fear of it.

Children raised around a father's anger become watchful in a way that never fully leaves them. They learn to read his mood the moment he walks in the door, to gauge the weather, to walk carefully, to keep the peace at the cost of their own peace. They become experts in a father's face, because their safety depends on it, and this vigilance becomes wired into them and follows them into adulthood, into their relationships, into their picture of God. A child who grew up managing an angry father often grows into an adult who cannot rest, who is always scanning for the anger of others, who relates to God as one more unpredictable authority whose mood must be managed. The father's anger does not stay in the room where it happened. It goes down into the child and shapes a life.

A father's anger does not stay in the room. It teaches a child to be watchful for a lifetime, and it hands them a God whose mood must be managed.

I should add that there is a place, for many men, where the work of dealing with anger requires more than self examination alone, and it is no shame to seek it. When a man's anger is rooted in old and serious wounds, in trauma he has never processed, in patterns laid down by his own father's rage, the honest naming of what is underneath may open onto a depth that needs the help of a wise counselor or a trusted pastor to walk through. Seeking that help is not a failure of faith or of manhood. It is the same courage that any healing requires, the willingness to let another person into the wounded place, and the man who seeks it is not weaker than the man who white knuckles alone. He is wiser, and his family will reap the difference.

There is a particular cruelty in the fact that this anger lands hardest on exactly the people a man most loves and least intends to harm. He does not explode at his boss, who could fire him, or at the stranger who could hit back. He explodes at his wife and his children, the ones who are safe, the ones who will not retaliate, the ones bound to him by love and therefore unable to defend themselves against him. The very safety of the family becomes the reason the family receives the worst of him, and this is a bitter irony that every honest man must face. The people who should be safest with him are, because of his anger, the least safe, and the bond of love that should have protected them is precisely what exposed them.

This is why the redemption of a man's anger is not a private matter of his own peace of mind. It is a matter of the souls he is shaping, of whether his children will grow up able to rest or forever watchful, of whether they will meet God as a refuge or as one more temper to be managed. A man who understands what his anger is doing to the people who receive it has a reason to fight it that mere self improvement could never supply. He is not just managing an unpleasant trait. He is protecting the souls he was given to protect, from himself, which is the hardest and most necessary protection a father ever offers.

I write about this as a man who has frightened people I love, who has watched my own sons go quiet and careful in the presence of my anger, and who has had to face that the anger was almost never about what I claimed it was about. It was about my fear, my shame, my exhaustion, my old unhealed places, and it came out sideways onto the smallest and safest people in my house because they could not fight back. The slow work of learning to find what my anger was hiding, and to bring the hidden thing to God and to trusted men instead of to my family, is some of the most important work I have ever done, and I am not finished with it. No man simply masters his temper and is done. But a man can learn what his temper is really made of, and that knowledge, brought again and again into the light, is where the redemption of a man's anger actually begins.

chapters.title: Men in Crisis
chapters.summary: The numbers are grim and the headlines are loud, but the crisis of men is not mainly a policy problem or a culture-war talking point. It is a crisis of meaning, and it has a specific shape.
chapters.body:
You have heard the statistics, and I am wary of leading with them, because a man is not a statistic and a crowd of suffering men is not an argument to be won. But the numbers exist and they are not neutral. Men are dying earlier, dropping out of school and work in growing numbers, disappearing from their children's lives, and dying by their own hand at rates that should stop every one of us cold. Something is wrong with how men are faring, and the wrongness is not evenly distributed, it is concentrated, and it is getting worse in the younger generations.

The trouble is that this crisis has been captured by the culture war, and once it was captured it stopped being a place of real help and became a place of scoring points. One side treats struggling men as villains getting their comeuppance. The other treats them as victims of a conspiracy against masculinity. Both are using these men rather than helping them, and I want to refuse both, and try to say something true and pastoral about what is actually happening to men and what actually helps.

The crisis is a crisis of meaning

Underneath the various symptoms, the drift and the despair and the disappearance, I believe there is a single root, and it is a crisis of meaning. A great many men no longer have a compelling answer to the question of what they are for. And a man without an answer to that question is a man in mortal danger, because men in particular seem to need a purpose to organize their lives around, something to serve that is larger than their own comfort, or they begin to come apart.

For most of human history, that answer was supplied automatically by circumstance. A man was for providing, for protecting, for building, for the survival of his family and his community, and the necessity of these things was obvious and daily. His usefulness was not in doubt, because the family would literally not eat if he did not act. The meaning was handed to him by the sheer hardness of existence.

Much of that automatic meaning has evaporated, and we have not replaced it. In a comfortable society, a man is not obviously necessary for survival. His physical strength is not required. His protection is rarely called upon. His provision, while helpful, is not the difference between life and death it once was. And into that vacuum of obvious purpose rushes the terrible question, what am I actually for. Many men cannot answer, and the unanswered question is corrosive, and it eats them slowly.

A man can survive almost any hardship if he knows what he is for. He cannot long survive comfort if he does not.

The false answers on offer

Into this vacuum a great many false answers have rushed, and they are profitable, and they are everywhere, and they are eating young men alive. There is the answer of domination, sold by a whole industry of men who tell the lost and hungry that meaning is found in wealth and status and the subjugation of women, that the way to be a man is to take, to conquer, to accumulate, to look down. It is an old lie in new packaging, and it appeals precisely because it offers the desperate man a clear script when he had none.

There is the answer of grievance, which tells the struggling man that his suffering is entirely someone else's fault, that he is the victim of a war against men, and that the solution is resentment. This one is seductive because it contains a grain of truth, the culture has at times been contemptuous of men, but it converts a real observation into a total identity, and a man built on grievance is a man who has outsourced his agency to his enemies and will never build anything.

And there is the answer of retreat, the quietest and perhaps the most common, in which the man simply withdraws. He gives up on ambition, on relationship, on responsibility, and disappears into the endless anesthetics available to him, the screens and the games and the substances, a slow soft surrender that looks like nothing much from the outside and is in fact a man dying by inches. This is the one that ends, too often, in the statistics I did not want to lead with.

What the false answers have in common

Notice what unites domination and grievance and retreat. Every one of them turns the man inward, toward himself. Domination is about my status. Grievance is about my victimhood. Retreat is about my comfort. In each case the self is the center, and the man is trying to solve the crisis of meaning by attending more furiously to himself, and it never works, because the self is precisely the wrong place to look. Meaning is not found by turning inward. A self curved in on itself is the definition of the very disease.

Every false answer to the crisis of meaning has one thing in common. It sends the man deeper into himself, which is the last place meaning has ever been found.

This is why the therapeutic culture, for all its genuine goods, cannot finally cure this. It keeps sending the man back to himself, to his feelings and his healing and his self actualization, when the man's deepest need is to be summoned out of himself toward something worth dying for. You do not heal a man in crisis by helping him love himself more. You heal him by giving him something large enough to lose himself in.

The particular danger of the young man

I want to speak specifically about the young men, because the crisis falls hardest on them and the counterfeits reach them first. A young man arrives at the threshold of adulthood with an enormous, unfocused energy and a deep, mostly unconscious need to know what he is for, and he finds a culture that has almost nothing coherent to say to him. The old scripts have been discredited, sometimes rightly, but nothing has been offered in their place, and so he stands in a vacuum of purpose at exactly the age when the need for purpose is most acute.

Into that vacuum the loudest voices rush, and they are almost never good voices. They are the voices selling domination, the voices selling grievance, the voices offering the young man a clear and flattering story about what a man is at the very moment he is most desperate for one. He is not drawn to these voices because he is wicked. He is drawn to them because he is starving, and they are offering food, and no one else is offering anything at all. The church, which should have the most compelling answer to the question of what a man is for, has too often been silent, or has offered the young man a tame and weightless Christianity that speaks to nothing in him.

We should feel the urgency of this. A generation of young men is being formed by the worst possible influences, not because those influences are so powerful but because the alternatives have gone quiet. The answer is not to compete with the counterfeits on their own flattering terms, offering young men a Christian version of dominance or a Christian version of grievance. The answer is to offer them the one thing the counterfeits cannot, a purpose worth a whole life, a summons out of themselves and into the service of something eternal, a manhood defined by the laying down of life rather than the seizing of it. That answer has weight, and young men are looking for weight, and if we will not give it to them, the men selling poison certainly will.

The answer that actually holds

So what is the true answer to what a man is for. Here I must speak as a Christian and a pastor, because I have watched the counterfeits fail and I have watched one thing hold. The true answer runs in the exact opposite direction from every counterfeit. A man is for laying his life down. He is for pouring himself out in the service of others, for a family, for a community, for a mission, for a God worth everything. His meaning is found not by grasping but by giving, not by accumulating but by spending himself, not by turning inward but by being drawn entirely outward toward something and Someone larger than himself.

This is why the crisis of men is, at bottom, a spiritual crisis, and why the merely political and psychological answers cannot reach it. A man was made to worship, made to serve, made to give himself away to something transcendent, and when that vertical dimension is stripped out, no amount of horizontal adjustment can fill the hole. You can improve his job prospects and his mental health and his relational skills, and these are all worth doing, but if he still does not know what he is ultimately for, the hole remains, and the hole is where the despair lives.

The church that failed to be a place for them

I have to turn the indictment toward my own house, because the church has too often been part of the problem rather than the answer. We have, in many places, produced a version of Christianity that seems to have nothing to say to a man in this particular crisis, that speaks to comfort rather than to purpose, that offers a man reassurance when what he needs is a summons. A man in the grip of the crisis of meaning walks into a church and often finds nothing that addresses the actual hole in him, no vision large enough to organize his life around, no call to lay himself down for something that matters, only a general encouragement to be a bit nicer and to attend more regularly.

This is a tragedy, because the church holds the one answer the man is actually looking for. We have the summons he needs, the call out of himself and into the service of an eternal kingdom, the purpose vast enough to hold a whole life, and we have too often buried it under a weightless niceness that speaks to nothing in a man dying for lack of a mission. The men who should be finding their answer in the church are instead finding the counterfeits, because the counterfeits at least speak to the actual hunger, however poisonously, while the church speaks to a hunger the man does not have.

The church holds the one answer to the crisis of meaning, and too often buries it under a niceness that speaks to nothing in a man dying for a mission.

And we have to stop being afraid of asking hard things of men, because the fear of demanding too much has made us demand nothing, and nothing is precisely what fails to reach a man in crisis. The counterfeits succeed in part because they ask a great deal. They demand discipline, sacrifice, allegiance, and men respond to being asked for much, because being asked for much implies that they are capable of much, that they matter, that their lives can bear weight. A church that asks nothing of men communicates, without meaning to, that nothing much is expected of them, and a man starving to be significant hears in that low expectation a confirmation of his own worthlessness. The gospel asks everything, and that is part of its power, and we have been too timid to say so.

If we are serious about the crisis of men, then we in the church have to recover the weight of what we actually believe and hold it out to men with the seriousness it deserves. Not a Christianity of comfort but a Christianity of costly purpose. Not a call to be pleasant but a call to die, to lay down a life in the service of something worth everything, which is precisely the call a man in crisis is most desperate to receive. The gospel is not weightless, and when it is preached with its full weight, it turns out to be exactly the thing a man in the crisis of meaning has been searching for the whole time.

I will not pretend this is a tidy solution to a vast and tangled crisis, and I distrust anyone who offers men a simple fix to a wound this deep. There are policy dimensions and economic dimensions and cultural dimensions, and they all matter, and I am not waving them away. But underneath all of it is a man asking what he is for, and finding no answer, and dying a little more each year that the question goes unanswered. To that man, the church has the one thing the whole marketplace of counterfeits cannot offer. Not a technique. A purpose vast enough to hold a life, in the service of a God who gave his own life first. I have seen that purpose pull men back from the edge when nothing else could. It is the truest thing I know to say to a man in crisis, and I say it as a man who was once, in my own way, that man.

chapters.title: Middle School: Identity, Belonging, and the Wilderness
chapters.summary: Middle school is a wilderness, and every child has to cross it. Your job is not to spare them the desert. It is to remain reachable while they wander through it.
chapters.body:
If there is a season of parenting that humbled me more than any other, it was the middle school years. Because that is when the child you knew begins, in front of you, to become someone you do not yet know, and the tools that worked when they were small stop working, and no new tools have arrived to replace them. You are parenting a stranger who used to be your baby, and the stranger is watching you to see if you can be trusted with who they are becoming.

I have crossed this wilderness five times. It never got easier, only more familiar. Each of my sons entered middle school as a known quantity and emerged three years later as a person I had to get to know all over again. And the years in between were a test, not of them, but of me, of whether I could love a moving target, whether I could stay present to a child who was pushing me away precisely because they needed to know I would not leave.

The wilderness is not a detour

We treat adolescence as a problem to be managed, a rough patch to survive, a detour off the road of healthy development. But the wilderness has always been where formation happens. Israel did not go around the desert. Israel went through it, and the going through was the point. The wilderness is where a people learns who they are when the old securities are stripped away and the promised land is not yet in sight.

Middle school is that desert for a child. The securities of childhood, the unquestioned belonging in the family, the simple faith, the comfort in their own skin, all of it gets stripped away at once. The body changes without permission. The friend group fractures. The faith that was a warm blanket starts to feel like a costume. And the child stands in the middle of all this loss, disoriented, and looks to you not to fix it but to prove that you will not abandon them in it.

You cannot spare your child the wilderness, and you should not want to. The desert is where a borrowed faith either becomes their own or reveals that it was never anything but yours.

The prophetic imagination that Walter Brueggemann spent his life describing began in the wilderness, in the place of disorientation, where the old certainties failed and something new had to be born. There is no shortcut through this. A faith that has never been disoriented has never had the chance to become the person's own. When we try to spare our children the wilderness, when we rush them through it or pretend it is not happening, we deny them the very crucible in which mature faith is forged. The desert is not a failure of the journey. The desert is the journey.

Belonging becomes everything

The great hunger of the middle school years is belonging. A younger child belongs by default, to the family, without effort or anxiety. But the adolescent brain reorganizes around the peer group with an intensity that can look, from the outside, like betrayal. Suddenly what the friends think matters more than what you think. What the group is doing matters more than what is wise. And a parent, watching this, can feel replaced.

You are not replaced. You are being temporarily deprioritized so that your child can do the necessary work of learning to belong outside the family, which is a skill they will need for the rest of their life. But this hunger for belonging is also where a middle schooler is most vulnerable. They will do almost anything to belong somewhere, and if they cannot find belonging in a healthy place, they will find it in an unhealthy one. The child excluded at church who finds welcome in a destructive crowd is not choosing destruction. They are choosing belonging, which is the deeper need, and taking the destruction as the price.

This is why the community of faith matters so intensely at this age, and why we so often get it wrong. If the church is a place where a middle schooler feels judged, uncool, out of place, or merely tolerated, we have handed them a reason to leave that has nothing to do with theology and everything to do with the deepest need of their developmental stage. A middle schooler will keep a faith that gives them belonging. They will shed a faith that leaves them lonely. We would do well to spend less energy defending our doctrine to our adolescents and more energy making sure they have somewhere to belong within the family of faith.

The performance of not caring

Middle schoolers become experts at performing indifference. My sons would come home from youth group and answer every question with one word. Fine. Nothing. I dunno. The eye roll became a second language. And in those years I made the mistake, more than once, of reading the performance as the reality. I saw the indifference and believed it, and pulled back, and left my son alone in exactly the moment he needed me to keep pursuing without smothering.

Because the indifference is a test. Not a manipulative one, a developmental one. The child pushes to see if you will stay. They perform not caring to find out whether your care is conditional on their responsiveness. And if you take the performance at face value and withdraw, you confirm their deepest fear, that your love was contingent, that it required their cooperation to survive. But if you keep showing up, keep asking, keep making the sandwich and offering the ride and sitting quietly in the room, you tell them something they cannot yet say they need to hear. You are stuck with me. I am not going anywhere. My love does not require your approval to keep coming.

Learning to read past the performance is one of the hardest skills of parenting an adolescent. The signals they send are almost always the opposite of what they need. The child who pushes hardest often needs your presence most. The one who says leave me alone is frequently testing whether you will. This does not mean you smother them or refuse to give them space. It means you learn the difference between a request for genuine distance and a test of your durability, and you learn to keep loving through the years when the love seems to land on a surface that will not absorb it. It is absorbing more than you know. It is just doing so silently, beneath a performance of indifference that is itself a form of trust.

Consider how much trust it actually takes for a child to show you their indifference rather than their eagerness to please. The child who performs not caring in front of you is a child who feels safe enough to stop performing goodness, safe enough to be difficult, safe enough to test the load-bearing capacity of your love. That is not the behavior of a child who has given up on you. It is the behavior of a child who is counting on you, who is using you as the fixed point against which they can push while they figure out who they are. The compliant child who never pushes may be the more worrying one, because their compliance may hide a fear that your love could not survive their honesty. The middle schooler who lets you see their worst is, in a strange and backward way, paying you a compliment. They are trusting you with the parts of themselves they hide from everyone else, and the trust deserves to be honored, not punished.

Identity under construction

The middle school years are when identity moves from something given to something built. The child is trying on selves, sometimes several in a week. This is bewildering to watch. The son who was athletic now wants to be artistic. The one who loved church now wears black and questions everything. And a parent, anxious for the child to turn out a certain way, can panic and try to lock down an identity before the construction is done.

Do not lock it down. The self your middle schooler is trying on this month is not necessarily the self they will keep. They are experimenting, and experimentation requires the freedom to try things that do not fit. When you react with alarm to every new phase, you teach them that self-discovery is dangerous, that becoming a person is something to be done in secret, away from your anxious eyes. The most stabilizing thing you can offer a middle schooler constructing an identity is a parent who is not threatened by the construction, who can watch them try on a dozen selves without treating any of them as a verdict.

The self your child performs in middle school is a rough draft, not a final copy. Panic over the draft, and you teach them to hide the writing.

Erik Erikson named this the central crisis of adolescence, the search for identity against the threat of confusion, and he understood that it cannot be rushed or resolved from the outside. A young person has to arrive at their own sense of who they are, and the arriving requires a moratorium, a protected space in which to experiment without permanent consequences. The parent who provides that space, who can tolerate the uncertainty, who refuses to foreclose the search prematurely by demanding an identity before the child is ready to have one, gives their child one of the great gifts of the middle school years.

Faith goes quiet, and that is not death

Perhaps the hardest thing for a Christian parent is watching the faith go quiet. The child who prayed easily now resists prayer. The one who loved the songs now stares at the wall. And the fear rises, the fear that you are losing them, that the faith you worked to build is crumbling in front of you.

But faith going quiet is not the same as faith dying. Often it is faith going underground to do its deepest work. The middle schooler cannot yet articulate the questions churning inside them, and so they go silent, and the silence is not absence but incubation. What is happening below the surface is the slow, invisible work of a child deciding whether any of this is theirs. You cannot see this work. You can only refuse to interrupt it with your anxiety.

I interrupted it more than once. I saw the quiet and filled it with pressure, with more devotions, more accountability, more anxious checking on the state of my son's soul. And the pressure did exactly what pressure does. It drove the process further underground, made him better at hiding, taught him that his real spiritual life was not safe to show me. What I should have done was trust the quiet, keep the relationship warm, and let the underground work happen without demanding to inspect it. The seed does its work in the dark, unseen, and the gardener who digs it up to check on its progress kills the very thing they were trying to nurture.

Staying reachable

The whole task of parenting a middle schooler, if I had to compress it into one thing, is staying reachable. Not controlling. Not fixing. Not managing the outcome. Just remaining a person your child can reach when they finally decide to reach. This means enduring the years when they do not reach, when the door stays closed, when your love seems to bounce off a surface that will not let it in.

You keep loving anyway. You keep the light on. You resist the urge to force your way in, because forcing only makes the door heavier, and you resist the urge to give up, because giving up confirms the abandonment they half-expect. You wait in the wilderness with them, reachable, patient, refusing to leave. And one day, not on your schedule, they turn around and reach, and you are there, because you never left.

The parent's own wilderness

What no one told me is that a child's wilderness triggers a wilderness in the parent. When your middle schooler stops needing you the way they used to, you face your own crisis of identity, your own loss of a role that gave your days meaning. The parent of a small child is needed constantly, urgently, in a way that is exhausting and also, quietly, deeply gratifying. The parent of a middle schooler is being fired from that role, slowly, and the firing hurts, and the hurt can curdle into a grasping that makes everything worse.

I had to do my own desert work in those years, had to face the ways I had built my sense of worth on being needed by my children, had to let God reshape my identity so that it did not depend on my sons requiring me. Because a parent who needs to be needed will unconsciously keep a child dependent, will resist the very growth they claim to want, will make the child responsible for the parent's sense of purpose. The healthiest thing I could offer my sons in their wilderness was a father who was doing his own wilderness work, who was finding his identity in God rather than in their dependence, and who was therefore free to release them without clinging. You cannot give a child room to grow if their growth threatens your reason for being. Do your own desert work, so that theirs is not burdened by yours.

My sons made it through the wilderness, each in his own time, each carrying a slightly different self out the other side than the one they carried in. And the thread that connected the boy who went into the desert to the young man who came out was not the faith I forced or the identity I preferred. It was the simple, stubborn fact that I stayed. In the wilderness, that is the whole of the job. Stay reachable. Do not leave. Let the desert do its work.

chapters.title: Parenting a Child with Special Needs
chapters.summary: The world measures children by what they achieve. A child with special needs exposes that measure as a lie, and reveals a gospel that never valued us for our productivity at all.
chapters.body:
I want to write about something I have witnessed closely in ministry but have not lived from the inside in the way that parents of children with special needs have lived it. So I write with a particular humility here, aware that there are things about this road that only those who walk it can fully know. But I have sat with enough of these families, in the hospital rooms and the therapy waiting areas and the quiet living rooms after the diagnosis, to have learned some things worth saying, and to have had my own theology broken open and rebuilt by what they taught me.

What I have learned, above all, is that a child with special needs exposes a lie that most of us live inside without ever noticing it. The lie is that human worth is tied to human achievement, that we matter because of what we can do, produce, accomplish, contribute. Our whole civilization is built on this lie, and most of our churches, whatever they say on Sunday, are built on it too. And a child who will never achieve by those measures stands as a living refutation of the whole system, and reveals a gospel that never valued any of us for our productivity in the first place.

The grief no one lets you name

Before anything else, there is grief, and it is a grief the world does not know how to let you have. When a child is born with, or later diagnosed with, a significant disability, a parent grieves. Not the child, who is loved fiercely and completely, but the loss of the imagined future, the expectations quietly assembled during the pregnancy, the life the parent had pictured that will now not be. This grief is real and it is legitimate, and yet parents are often made to feel they cannot voice it, because to grieve the imagined child seems like a rejection of the actual child.

It is not. A parent can love their child completely and still grieve the future they thought they would have. The two are not in conflict. The grief must be allowed to breathe, to be named, to be brought before God honestly, because grief that is suppressed does not disappear. It goes underground and poisons. The parents I have watched flourish in this calling are the ones who were permitted, by their community and by their own honesty, to grieve fully, and then to move through the grief into a love that was not diminished by having grieved. The church that tells such parents they should feel only blessing, only joy, only gratitude, robs them of the honesty their souls require.

You can love your child with your whole heart and still grieve the future you imagined. Do not let anyone shame you out of the grief. Grief honored becomes love deepened. Grief denied becomes love poisoned.

The grief does not resolve once and disappear. It returns, often, at the thresholds, at the birthday parties for other children, at the milestones that will not come, at the moment a younger sibling passes the older child in some capacity the older child will never reach. This recurring grief is not a failure of acceptance or a lack of faith. It is the ongoing cost of loving deeply in a world that is not yet what it will be, and it deserves to be met with tenderness, not with a demand that the parent should be over it by now.

The idol of the productive life

Our society has made an idol of productivity, and the idol demands human sacrifice. We measure a person's worth by their output, their achievement, their contribution to the economy and the accumulation of accomplishments. And this idol reaches into places we do not notice, including the way we love our children, the pride we take in their achievements, the quiet way we treat their accomplishments as a reflection of our own worth as parents.

A child with profound special needs cannot participate in this economy of worth, and their existence therefore functions as a prophetic word against it. Here is a human being, fully and completely a person, made in the image of God, precious beyond measure, who will never produce, achieve, or contribute in the ways the idol demands. And their preciousness is not one bit diminished by that fact. If we can see this clearly, we discover that the idol was always a lie, that human worth was never about productivity, that every one of us was loved by God before we produced anything and would be loved by God if we produced nothing at all.

A child who will never achieve by the world's measures is a prophet against the world's measures. Their worth, undiminished by their limitations, exposes the lie that any of our worth was ever about achievement.

Jean Vanier, who gave his life to communities where those with profound intellectual disabilities lived alongside those without, insisted that such persons were not merely recipients of care but bearers of a gift, that they revealed to the rest of us the poverty of our own hearts and the truth of our own dependence. Whatever we make of the failures that later came to light in his own life, the truth he pointed to remains, and it is a truth the church has been slow to receive. The person the world overlooks is often the one placed among us to heal us of the very blindness that makes us overlook them.

What the image of God actually means

We say that human beings are made in the image of God, but we often smuggle into that phrase an assumption that the image consists in our capacities, our reason, our will, our ability to do things. And if the image of God were located in our capacities, then a person with diminished capacities would bear a diminished image, which is a monstrous conclusion that the Scripture nowhere supports.

The image of God is not a set of abilities we possess. It is a status we are given, a dignity conferred by the Creator, a belonging that does not depend on what we can do. The theologian who taught me this most clearly insisted that the image is about being addressed by God, being in relationship, being held in the divine regard, and none of that depends on cognitive capacity or physical ability. A child who cannot speak, cannot reason as others reason, cannot care for themselves, bears the full and undiminished image of God, and is fully and completely a person whom God addresses and holds and loves. To see this is to have your entire theology of the human person corrected by a child the world would overlook.

The gift hidden in the dependence

There is a gift buried in the profound dependence of a child with severe special needs, though it is a gift wrapped in exhaustion and hard to receive. The gift is a truth about all of us that we spend our lives denying. We are all dependent. We all began in total helplessness and will very likely end there, and in between we sustain the illusion of self-sufficiency that our culture prizes. The child who never outgrows dependence holds up a mirror to the human condition that the rest of us work hard to avoid.

And the dependence, rightly seen, is not a defect but a revelation. It reveals that we were made for relationship, for receiving, for being held, and that the myth of the independent self is exactly that, a myth. The parent who cares for a fully dependent child is living inside a truth about love that the rest of us only glimpse, the truth that love is not a transaction between equals who exchange value, but a giving that asks nothing in return, that finds its meaning in the giving itself. This is, not incidentally, exactly how God loves us. We are all far more dependent on God than we admit, and the child who cannot pretend otherwise teaches the rest of us what we are.

There is a further truth hidden here that our achievement-obsessed culture cannot easily see. The child who receives and cannot repay is not the diminished partner in the relationship of love. In some ways they are the one who gives the greater gift, because they give the parent the chance to love without the corrupting motive of return, to love in the purest form love can take, the form that expects nothing back. We are so trained to think of the caregiver as the giver and the cared-for as the receiver that we miss the reciprocity that runs the other way. The child gives the parent an occasion to become a certain kind of person, a person capable of a love the world barely believes in, a love that most of us, tangled as we are in transactions, never fully learn. The one the world would call a burden is, in the deep economy of the soul, a giver of the rarest gift, the gift of an object for love that asks for nothing in return.

The siblings who also carry it

There is a dimension of this road that is easy to overlook, and it is the experience of the other children in the family, the siblings of the child with special needs. They grow up in a home where an enormous share of the family's time, energy, and attention is necessarily directed toward one child, and they learn, often, to ask for little, to make themselves easy, to carry needs of their own that go unspoken because they can see that their parents are already stretched to the breaking point.

These siblings often become remarkable people, marked by a compassion and a maturity beyond their years. But they also carry a hidden weight, and they need to be seen in it. They need a parent who notices that they too are children with needs, who finds moments to give them undivided attention, who does not allow their goodness and their ease to become an excuse for their neglect. And they need permission to feel the complicated things they feel, the love for their sibling tangled up with resentment, guilt, embarrassment, and grief, without being shamed for the feelings that are the honest fruit of a hard situation. A family raising a child with special needs is raising all its children in the shadow of that reality, and the ones without the diagnosis are shaped by it just as deeply, and deserve to be seen just as clearly.

The community that must show up

Here again the church is tested and often found wanting. Families raising children with special needs frequently find themselves isolated, exhausted, and quietly excluded from the life of a church that was not built with their child in mind. The service that cannot accommodate a child who makes noise. The children's ministry with no place for a child who does not fit the standard program. The well-meaning members who do not know what to say and so say nothing, and by their silence communicate that this family is a burden rather than a gift.

A church that believes what it says about the image of God will move heaven and earth to include these families, will build the ramps and train the volunteers and make the space, will treat the child with special needs not as a challenge to be accommodated but as a member of the body whose presence blesses the whole. The measure of a church's theology is not what it says about human dignity in the abstract but how it treats the child who cannot contribute in the currency the world values. If we cannot make room for that child, we have not understood the gospel we claim to preach.

The love that reveals God

I have watched parents of children with special needs love in a way that has taught me more about the love of God than most sermons I have heard, including my own. Because it is a love that expects nothing back, that gives and gives to a child who may never say thank you, may never understand the sacrifice, may never be able to reciprocate. And in that one-directional, cost-absorbing, expecting-nothing love, I have seen the clearest earthly picture of how God loves us.

God's love for us is not a response to our achievements or a reward for our contribution. It is a love that gives to those who can give nothing back, that pours out on the helpless and the dependent, that asks nothing and offers everything. The parent who loves a profoundly disabled child is not merely enduring a hardship. They are participating in the very heart of God, living out the divine love in the flesh, teaching the watching world what love actually is when it is stripped of transaction and reduced to its essence. If you are that parent, know this: you are not merely surviving. You are revealing God. And the child you love, whom the world would overlook, is one of the clearest windows into the kingdom that I know.

chapters.title: Parenting in the Digital Age: Screens, Souls, and Boundaries
chapters.summary: The screen is not neutral. It is designed to capture what we were meant to give to God and each other. Parenting through it requires more than filters. It requires formation.
chapters.body:
I raised my older sons before the smartphone and my younger sons after it, and the difference is one of the starkest natural experiments I have ever lived inside. The world my oldest navigated as a teenager and the world my youngest navigates are not the same world, and anyone who tells you the difference is merely a matter of new tools has not paid attention. The screen did not just give our children new things to do. It rewired the environment in which their souls are being formed.

I want to resist two easy responses here, because both let us off the hook. One is the panic that treats every screen as poison and every parent who allows one as negligent. The other is the shrug that treats the technology as neutral, just a tool, no different in kind from a book or a telephone. Neither is honest. The screen is not neutral, but the answer is not panic. The answer is formation, and formation is much harder than either fear or indifference.

The screen is designed, and not for your child's good

Let us begin with what we would rather not say. The devices in our children's hands were designed by some of the most brilliant minds of our time, funded by some of the largest fortunes ever assembled, for a single purpose: to capture and hold human attention. Not to inform. Not to connect. To capture. The business model depends on it. Every feature that keeps a child scrolling was engineered to keep them scrolling, and the engineers know exactly what they are doing, because they measure it.

This matters theologically, because attention is not a trivial thing. Attention is close to the center of the spiritual life. What we attend to shapes what we love, and what we love shapes who we become. Simone Weil said that attention, absolute unmixed attention, is prayer. And here is a machine, in your child's hand, engineered by an industry to fragment attention into ten-second pieces and sell those pieces to advertisers. We are not fighting a neutral tool. We are fighting a deliberate assault on the very faculty by which a soul learns to love God and neighbor.

The screen is not competing with your child's boredom. It is competing with their capacity for attention, and attention is the faculty by which they will one day learn to pray, to love, and to be present. This is a battle for something sacred.

The social psychologist Jonathan Haidt has documented the sharp inflection that arrived when the smartphone and the social platform reached the hands of adolescents, and the timing of the rise in anxiety, depression, and self-harm that followed it. Correlation is not the whole story, and honest people can argue about mechanisms. But the pattern is stark enough that no thoughtful parent can dismiss it, and it lines up with what any of us can observe in our own homes. Something has changed in the inner lives of the young, and the device in their pocket is somewhere near the center of it.

Filters are not formation

The first instinct of the anxious Christian parent is technical. Install the filter. Set the controls. Monitor the usage. And there is a place for these things, especially with younger children, because you do not hand a child a loaded environment and call it freedom. But filters address the wrong problem. Filters keep bad content out. They do nothing to form the soul that will one day, inevitably, encounter the bad content without a filter.

The goal is not a child who cannot access harm because you blocked it. The goal is a child who has been formed into a person who can navigate a world full of harm with wisdom and self-possession. And that formation does not come from software. It comes from the slow, relational work of teaching a child to understand what the screen is doing to them, to notice the pull, to develop the internal muscles of restraint that no external filter can substitute for. A child raised only on filters arrives at eighteen with no filter and no internal formation, which is the worst of both worlds.

This is not an argument against filters. It is an argument against relying on them. The filter buys time, and time is valuable, because it delays exposure until a child is more capable of handling it. But the time must be used, not merely bought. If the years behind the filter are not spent forming a child's judgment, their appetites, their capacity for self-restraint, then the filter has only postponed the reckoning, and the reckoning will arrive against a soul no more prepared for it than before.

What the screen displaces

The real cost of the screen is often not what it shows but what it displaces. Every hour on the device is an hour not spent in the activities that form a healthy soul. Boredom, which is the seedbed of imagination, is now instantly abolished at the first flicker of discomfort. Solitude, which is where a person learns to be at peace with their own company and, eventually, with God, is now impossible, because the device ensures no one is ever alone with their thoughts.

Face-to-face relationship, with all its friction and its irreplaceable richness, is thinned out and replaced by mediated connection that feels like relationship but delivers a fraction of its nourishment. And the developing brain, which needs deep rest, is instead kept in a state of low-grade stimulation late into the night. What the screen displaces is often more damaging than what it delivers. A childhood without boredom, without solitude, without unhurried presence, is a childhood missing the very conditions in which depth grows.

Ask not only what your child is consuming on the screen. Ask what the screen is preventing them from ever experiencing. The absence of boredom is not a gift. It is the theft of imagination.

Boredom is not the enemy we have made it out to be. Boredom is the doorway to imagination, to creativity, to the interior life. A child who is never bored never learns to generate their own inner world, never discovers that the most interesting thing available is not on a screen but inside their own restless, God-given mind. When we rush to eliminate every moment of boredom with a device, we are not being kind. We are amputating a faculty, and the child will grow up unable to be alone with themselves, terrified of the silence in which God is most often found.

The parent in the mirror

Here is where I must implicate myself, and where most of the parenting advice on this subject goes quiet, because it is more comfortable to talk about the children's screens than our own. My children learned their relationship with the screen partly by watching mine. When I checked my phone at dinner, I taught them that the meal was less important than whatever was in my hand. When I responded to a text mid-conversation with my son, I taught him that his father's attention was always provisional, always interruptible, always available to be claimed by someone else.

I cannot count the times a son was telling me something and I was half-present, my eyes drifting to the screen, my thumb already scrolling. I told myself I was listening. I was not. And a child knows the difference between a parent who is present and a parent who is performing presence while their attention is elsewhere. Before I lecture my children about their screen habits, I have to reckon with the fact that I formed those habits, in part, by the example of my own divided attention. The hypocrisy is not lost on them, and it should not be lost on us.

Boundaries as gifts, not punishments

When boundaries do come, and they must, the framing matters enormously. A boundary presented as a punishment, as distrust, as the parent asserting control, invites resistance and teaches the child that the screen is a prize being withheld. A boundary presented as a gift, as a protection of something valuable, as the family together choosing to guard its attention and its presence, invites participation.

The most effective boundaries are the ones the whole family keeps together. The phones that sleep outside the bedroom, all of them, the parents' included. The dinner table where no one, adult or child, brings a device. The stretch of Sabbath where the whole household unplugs together. These are not rules imposed from above. They are practices the family embraces together, and they form everyone, including the parents who most need forming. A child who watches their father put his own phone away for the sake of presence learns something no lecture could teach.

Forming the appetite, not just restricting the intake

Ultimately, parenting in the digital age is about forming an appetite, not just restricting an intake. A child who is only restricted, only blocked, only told no, develops a hunger for the forbidden thing and a plan to access it the moment they are free. A child whose appetites are being formed toward better things, who has tasted the deep satisfaction of a long book, an unhurried conversation, a project made with their hands, a walk with nowhere to be, is developing an internal compass that will serve them when the external controls fall away.

This is the harder work, and the slower work, and the work that no app can do for you. It means providing the alternatives, the analog richness, the family culture in which the screen is not the default but one option among many that are actually more compelling. It means being present enough, unhurried enough, un-distracted enough yourself, that your presence is more attractive than the device. That last one indicts me most of all, because a child will not choose the parent over the screen if the parent is always half inside a screen of their own.

The comparison machine and the young soul

There is a particular harm the screen does to the adolescent soul that deserves naming on its own, because it is more insidious than the obvious dangers we warn about. The platforms our children inhabit are comparison machines. They present, endlessly, a curated highlight reel of everyone else's life, against which the ordinary reality of the child's own life cannot help but look impoverished. A young person scrolling through the polished, filtered, carefully staged images of their peers is being fed, hour after hour, the lie that everyone else is happier, more beautiful, more included, more successful than they are.

This is spiritual poison of a specific kind. Envy has always been a threat to the soul, but never before has a machine been engineered to manufacture envy at industrial scale and deliver it directly into the mind of a developing child. The old wisdom that we should not compare ourselves to others was hard enough to follow when comparison meant the few neighbors we could see. Now the comparison is with a curated infinity, an endless feed of everyone's best moment, and the young soul measures its ordinary Tuesday against a thousand highlight reels and concludes that it is failing. To form a child who can resist this is to form a child who knows their worth does not come from the feed, who can look away, who can be content with an unremarkable life that is nonetheless their own and nonetheless loved by God.

There is another layer to this that cuts even deeper, and it is the way the platforms teach a young person to perform their own life rather than to live it. When every experience is potential content, when the value of a moment is measured by how it will look to an audience, the child learns to stand outside their own life, curating it, packaging it, watching themselves be watched. This is a kind of exile from the self, a loss of the capacity to simply be present in an experience without the running commentary of how it will play. A young person formed this way loses something precious, the ability to have an experience that belongs only to them, unphotographed, unposted, unwitnessed by anyone but God. To give your child moments that are not content, experiences that exist only for their own sake, is to give them back a piece of their own soul that the platforms are quietly stealing. The unposted moment, the memory kept private, the joy that no one else sees, is a form of wealth the comparison machine cannot touch.

The digital age is not going away, and I am not calling you to pretend it is. I am calling you to something more demanding than filters and more honest than panic. I am calling you to form your children, and yourself, into people whose attention is not for sale, whose presence is not fragmented, whose souls are not colonized by an industry that profits from their distraction. That formation begins with the phone in your own hand. Put it down. Look at your child. Be there. The most radical thing you can do in the digital age is to give your child your undivided attention, because you will be teaching them, by doing it, what they are worth.

chapters.title: Parenting Toddlers: Foundation Before Performance
chapters.summary: The toddler years feel like survival, not discipleship. But what a two-year-old learns about whether the world is safe becomes the ground every later faith stands on.
chapters.body:
No one warns you that the most theologically significant years of your child's life may be the ones you barely remember because you were too exhausted to think. The toddler years are a blur of spilled milk and interrupted sleep and the particular despair of a tantrum in a grocery store. It does not feel like formation. It feels like survival. And yet what happens in these years lays down the deepest layer of a person, the layer that all later belief will either rest on or wrestle against.

I have watched five toddlers become five different men, and I can tell you that the version of me who parented the first toddler and the version who parented the fifth were not the same man. The first time, I was terrified and controlling. By the fifth, I was tired and, mercifully, a little wiser. What I learned across those years is that toddlers do not need us to perform. They need us to be a foundation. And a foundation does not perform. It holds.

The theology hidden in a peekaboo game

When a toddler learns that the parent who leaves the room comes back, something enormous is happening. The child is learning what the psychologists call object permanence, but they are also learning something deeper. They are learning that absence is not abandonment. That the one who goes away returns. That the world can be trusted to give back what it takes.

This is not a small thing dressed up as a big thing. This is the seedbed of faith. Before a child can believe in a God they cannot see, they must first learn that things unseen are still real, still there, still coming back. The peekaboo game, silly as it is, rehearses the very structure of trust that faith will one day require. A child who learns reliability at two has a place to put faith at twelve. A child who learns that the world is unpredictable and adults disappear without warning has to overcome that formation before faith can take root.

You are not just keeping a toddler alive. You are teaching a soul whether the universe can be trusted. Every time you come back, you preach a sermon they will not remember and never forget.

The research on early attachment, going back to the work of John Bowlby and the generations of scholars who followed him, keeps arriving at the same conclusion from a hundred different angles. The child who experiences a caregiver as a secure base, reliably present, reliably responsive, develops a fundamental posture toward existence that is trusting rather than defended. This posture is laid down below language, below memory, in the body itself. And whatever theology that child later encounters will be received by a soul already shaped either to trust or to guard. We are writing on our children before they can read what we write.

The tyranny of the well-behaved child

Somewhere along the way, Christian parenting culture absorbed a value that has nothing to do with the gospel: the well-behaved child as evidence of good parenting. The quiet toddler in church. The one who sits still, who does not interrupt, who performs calm. We reward this, and we judge ourselves against it, and in doing so we teach our children the most anti-gospel lesson possible, that love is earned by performance.

I confess I wanted well-behaved sons. In part because I loved them and wanted them to flourish, but in part, if I am honest, because their behavior was a report card on me. When my toddler melted down in the church lobby, I felt exposed, judged, found out as a fraud who could not control his own house. And in that shame, I would correct him not for his sake but for mine. I was managing my reputation through my child's behavior. That is not discipline. That is using a two-year-old to protect my ego.

A toddler is supposed to melt down. A toddler has a nervous system that has not yet learned to regulate itself, and the whole point of these years is that the child borrows your regulation until they can grow their own. When you stay calm in the face of the storm, you are not just surviving the tantrum. You are lending your steadiness to a small person who does not have any yet. That is the work. It is invisible, it is exhausting, and it is holy. The parent who can remain a non-anxious presence in the face of a screaming child is doing something far more formative than the parent who successfully produces silence through fear.

Grace before they can understand grace

Here is what moves me about parenting a toddler. You extend grace to a person who cannot yet comprehend it. You forgive before they can ask. You keep loving through the phase where they hit you, bite you, scream that they hate you and want the other parent. And in doing so, you enact the gospel toward a person who has no theology to make sense of it.

They will not remember these specific moments. But the pattern sinks below memory into the body. The child who is met with warmth after wrongdoing learns, in their bones, that wrongdoing does not end love. Long before they can define grace, they will have lived inside it. And when someone later tells them that God is like this, that God's love is not withdrawn by their failure, some deep part of them will recognize it, because it will feel like home.

This is why the toddler years, exhausting as they are, matter so much for what a child will one day be able to believe. Grace is difficult to accept for anyone raised to believe love is conditional. If a child's earliest and deepest experience of being loved was an experience of love that had to be earned through good behavior, then the gospel of unearned grace will run against the grain of everything they know, and they will spend years fighting to believe what should be good news. But a child who lived inside unconditional love from the beginning has a place to receive the gospel, because the gospel will sound like the truth they already lived.

Foundation is not the same as leniency

Let me be careful here, because grace is easily counterfeited as permissiveness. A foundation holds, and holding requires boundaries. The toddler who is allowed to do anything is not being loved. They are being abandoned to their own chaos, and chaos frightens a small child even when they are the ones creating it. Boundaries are not the opposite of grace. Boundaries are a form of it. The fence around the yard is what makes the yard safe to play in.

So you say no. You remove them from the danger. You hold the line on the things that matter. But you hold it without contempt, without shame, without the withdrawal of your affection. The no and the love arrive together. This is the hardest thing to do when you are exhausted, because exhaustion strips away our patience and leaves the raw material of our anger. I lost my temper with my toddlers more times than I want to count. The recovery, the coming back, the getting down on their level and saying I was wrong to yell, that was the real formation. Not my failure. My return after the failure.

A parent who never fails their toddler teaches nothing about grace. A parent who fails and then repairs teaches everything. The repair is the sermon.

What a small child needs is not a perfect parent, which does not exist, but a parent who ruptures and repairs, who fails and returns, who loses patience and comes back with tenderness. The relational scientists call this rupture and repair, and they have found that it is not the absence of rupture that builds security but the reliable presence of repair. Every time you come back after failing your toddler, you teach them that relationships survive failure, that love is durable, that a bond can be broken and mended. That is a lesson they will draw on for the rest of their lives, in every relationship they ever have, including their relationship with God.

The exhaustion is not a distraction from the work

For a long time I treated the fatigue of the toddler years as an obstacle to spiritual life. I could not pray the way I used to. I could not read the way I used to. My devotional life, once orderly, was in ruins. I felt like I had lost God in the noise. What I did not understand then, and understand now, is that the noise was the field of formation, mine as much as theirs.

The self-emptying required to parent a toddler is a school of the soul. You are woken at three in the morning by someone who cannot say thank you and will not for years. You give and give and receive tantrums in return. This is not a distraction from the spiritual life. This is the spiritual life, taught to you by a person in diapers. God was not absent in those years. God was in the getting up at three in the morning, teaching me a love that does not keep score, that does not require gratitude to keep giving. I was being discipled by my own children, though I would not have described it that way at the time, because at the time I mostly just wanted to sleep.

What I would tell a younger father

If I could reach the version of myself who was drowning in the toddler years, I would tell him a few things. I would tell him to stop measuring. Stop checking whether he was doing it right. The measuring was making him anxious, and his anxiety was contagious, and his toddlers were catching it. A calm parent is worth more than a correct one.

I would tell him that the goal of these years is not obedience. It is attachment. A securely attached child will grow into obedience because they trust the one who leads them. A child driven to obedience without attachment learns compliance and stores up resentment. Build the bond first. The behavior follows the bond, not the other way around.

I would tell him that the sleepless nights are not lost time. They are deposits into an account he cannot see, and one day, when his son is grown and calls him just to talk, he will understand that the man on the other end of the line was formed, in part, in the dark hours when nobody was watching and no one said thank you.

And I would tell him one more thing, the thing I most needed to hear and did not have anyone to say it. I would tell him that he is allowed to find it hard. That the exhaustion and the frustration and the occasional flash of resentment do not make him a bad father or a bad Christian. The sanitized picture of parenting that circulates in Christian circles, all gratitude and wonder and precious moments, is a lie that isolates the parent who is actually drowning. The toddler years are genuinely hard, and the honest father who admits it is closer to grace than the pretending father who performs a joy he does not feel. God is not disappointed in the tired parent. God is near to them, in the getting up again, in the choosing to love when the feeling of love has been ground down by fatigue. That choosing, when the feeling is gone, is the deepest love of all, and it is the love that most resembles the love of God, who keeps loving us through every night we give him nothing back.

The performance we owe no one

There is a particular exhaustion that comes not from the toddler but from the audience, real or imagined, that we believe is watching us parent. The mother in the grocery store who feels the eyes of strangers on her screaming child. The father at church who reads judgment in every glance. We parent, too often, for an audience, and the audience is merciless, and the audience does not love our children or us. The performance we put on for the audience drains the very energy we need for the actual work, which has no audience at all, which happens in the dark and the ordinary and the unwitnessed hours.

I have come to believe that the freedom to stop performing is one of the great graces of the gospel applied to parenting. We are not on trial. Our children's behavior is not a verdict on our worth. God does not grade us on the compliance of our toddlers, and neither should we grade ourselves. The parent who is freed from the performance can be present to the child in a way the performing parent never can, because the performing parent is always half-turned toward the audience, and the child feels that turning, and knows they do not have the parent's whole face. Put the audience out of your mind. There is only you, and this small person, and the God who sees what no audience sees.

The toddler years feel like they will never end, and then, abruptly, they are over, and you would give a great deal to have one more ordinary morning of it back. Build the foundation while you can. Not the performance. The foundation. The quiet, unmemorable, world-shaping work of being the reliable love a small person learns to trust. Everything later is built on it, and nothing later can be built on anything else.

chapters.title: Raising Daughters in a World That Objectifies Them
chapters.summary: I have five sons and no daughters, which means I write this as an outsider to the specific war being waged on the girls in your house. But I have watched the war, and I know the lie at the center of it.
chapters.body:
I have five sons and no daughters. I want to say that at the top, because it would be a kind of dishonesty to write about raising daughters as if I had done it. I have not. What I have done is pastor the fathers and mothers of daughters for fifteen years, watch the girls in my congregation grow up inside a machine that means them harm, and raise five boys who are, whether I like it or not, part of the world those girls have to survive. So I write this from beside the problem rather than inside it, and I write it partly as a confession, because the sons I am raising are being formed by the same machine, on the other side of it, to consume what it teaches them to see.

The machine has a name, or several. The academic term is the sexual objectification of women, and the developmental research on it is now substantial enough that I do not have to speculate. The girls in your house are being trained, from an age earlier than you think, to experience themselves as things to be looked at. That is the war. And the church has too often responded to it with a counter-lie that is only the same lie in a longer skirt.

The name for what is happening to her

In 1997, two psychologists, Barbara Fredrickson and Tomi-Ann Roberts, published a paper in the journal Psychology of Women Quarterly that named the mechanism with unusual precision. They called it objectification theory, and its central claim is this: when a culture persistently treats girls and women as bodies to be evaluated by others, the girls internalize the outside gaze. They begin to watch themselves from the outside. They stop asking what does my body feel and start asking what does my body look like to someone watching. Fredrickson and Roberts called this self-objectification, and their research, replicated many times since, linked it to a cluster of afflictions that fall disproportionately on girls: anxiety, depression, disordered eating, and a diminished ability to be present in one's own life because part of the mind is always occupied monitoring one's appearance.

Sit with the horror of that for a moment. A girl learns to spend a permanent fraction of her attention watching herself be watched. She is never fully inside her own experience, because a portion of her is always outside it, checking the picture. And the machine that trains her, the advertising, the algorithms, the pornographic wallpaper of the culture, the filtered images that even her friends are posting, does this to her before she is old enough to name it or resist it. This is not a moral panic. It is measured, published, and replicated developmental psychology, and it describes a genuine assault on the interior life of the girls we are raising.

She is taught to watch herself being watched, until a part of her is always standing outside her own life, checking the picture. That is not vanity. It is an injury, and it is being inflicted on purpose.

The church's counter-lie

Here is where I have to turn on my own house, because the church saw this assault and often responded with something that was not the gospel but its counterfeit. It responded with the purity culture of the 1990s and 2000s, and I watched that culture form a generation of girls, and I have since counseled the women it wounded.

The counter-lie went like this. The world says your body is a thing to be looked at and consumed. The church replied: yes, your body is a thing to be looked at, and therefore you must cover it, guard it, and manage it, because it is a stumbling block, a temptation, a danger to the boys around you. Do you hear what happened? The church accepted the world's basic premise, that the girl's value and meaning are located in her body as an object of the male gaze, and then simply reversed the instruction. The world said display it; the church said hide it. But both agreed on the thing that mattered: she is, first and fundamentally, a body that men will look at, and her spiritual task is to manage that looking.

The fruit of this was bitter, and I have tasted it in my office. Women raised in purity culture who could not experience their own bodies as good even inside a marriage the church itself had blessed, because they had been trained to see their bodies as landmines. Women who carried shame for having been looked at, as if the looking were their sin. Women who had been told, in youth group, that their bodies were the reason a boy might fall, which placed on a fourteen-year-old girl the responsibility for the imagination of every boy who saw her. That is a monstrous burden, and it is the same objectification the world practices, baptized and handed back to her as holiness. We did not free her from the gaze. We just added God's name to it.

What Scripture actually says about the daughter's body

The recovery is not a better modesty policy. It is a different anthropology, and it is right there in the text we claimed to be defending.

The first thing Scripture says about the human body, male and female, is that it was made in the image of God. "So God created man in his own image, in the image of God he created him; male and female he created them" (Genesis 1:27). The daughter's body is not first an object of anyone's gaze. It is first an image of God, a bearer of divine likeness, made to be a subject who looks out at the world and acts within it, not primarily an object that is looked at. Every regime that reduces her to a thing to be evaluated, whether it hands her a bikini or a burden of blame, is denying Genesis 1:27, and the church that adopted the world's premise denied it too.

And Scripture is relentless that the value of a person is not in the surface the world evaluates. "Charm is deceitful, and beauty is vain, but a woman who fears the Lord is to be praised" (Proverbs 31:30). Peter writes to women that their true adornment is not the external, the braided hair and the gold, but "the hidden person of the heart with the imperishable beauty of a gentle and quiet spirit, which in God's sight is very precious" (1 Peter 3:3-4). Read that phrase carefully, because purity culture abused it too: in God's sight. The verse relocates the audience. The girl trained by the machine performs for the gaze of the watching world. Peter tells her the audience that matters is God, who sees the hidden person and not the surface, and who has already declared her precious before she managed a single thing about her appearance. That is not another instruction about how to be looked at. It is an escape from the whole economy of being looked at.

What I am trying to do with my sons

I said this was a confession, and here is the confessing part. The war on daughters cannot be won on the daughters' side alone, because half the machine runs through boys, and I am raising five of them. The girls in your congregation will grow up into a world staffed by men, and some of those men will be mine, and the question of whether they consume women as objects or honor them as image-bearers is being decided right now, in my house, on my watch.

So the work I actually control is not the daughters' modesty. It is my sons' vision. I am trying, imperfectly and against the same machine, to raise boys who see a woman as a whole person before they see her as a body, who are not trained by a decade of pornographic saturation to evaluate before they encounter, who understand that the gaze the world taught them is not neutral looking but a habit of consumption that damages the person consumed and hollows out the one consuming. When Jesus said that a man who looks at a woman to lust for her has already committed adultery in his heart (Matthew 5:28), he located the sin where it belongs, in the one doing the looking, not the one being looked at. Purity culture inverted that verse and hung it on the girls. I am trying to hang it back where Christ put it, on the boys, on my boys, where the responsibility actually lives.

What a father is actually for

I came to faith from atheism, and I was raised without a father, and those two facts collide most sharply for me right here, because I am now the thing I never had, to sons who will help decide how a generation of daughters is treated. A girl raised with a father who delighted in her mind before her appearance, who was interested in what she thought and not merely how she looked, who was safe and present and did not leave, has been handed a set of instruments for detecting the counterfeit long before the counterfeit arrives. She has felt what it is to be loved as a person by a man, and so the man who wants to love her only as a body has a harder time convincing her that consumption is the same as care. She has a reference point. The absence of that reference point is one of the machine's quietest advantages, and I know it from the inside, because I grew up without the male love that would have taught me what love from a man was supposed to feel like.

The research bears this out with unusual consistency, and I state it carefully because the topic is prone to overreach. Studies of paternal involvement, including the work summarized by researchers like Ronald Rohner on the effects of father acceptance and rejection, have found across cultures that a father's warm, engaged presence correlates with better outcomes for daughters in self-image, in the timing and health of their relationships, and in their resistance to exploitation. This is not a promise, and it is not a mechanism a father can operate like a lever, because children are not machines and God is sovereign over ends no parent controls. But it points at something true and old: that the way a girl is treated by the first man who loves her shapes what she will tolerate from the men who come after. The father is a witness. His love is testimony, admitted into evidence long before she can weigh it, about whether a woman is a subject to be known or an object to be used.

God knew this about himself before any of us knew it about our fathers. The name he most insists on, over against every distortion, is Father, and the psalm calls him "Father of the fatherless and protector of widows" precisely at the point where the human father has failed or vanished (Psalm 68:5). I take that verse personally, because I was one of the fatherless it names, and I have staked my life on the claim that the God it describes is real. A daughter whose earthly father fails her, or dies, or was never there, is not therefore doomed, because there is a Father who does not leave, and the church that mediates his love to the fatherless girl is doing the most direct possible work against the machine. But where a human father is present, he is not off the hook. He is on the front line, and most of us do not treat the assignment with the seriousness the girls deserve.

The weight this leaves
