I cannot tell you how to raise your daughter, because I have never raised one, and I distrust the men who write confidently about a war they have only watched. But I can tell you what I have seen from beside it, and I can tell you the one thing I would stake everything on.

Your daughter is being told, by a machine of enormous power and no conscience, that she is a surface. The world says the surface should be displayed. Some of the church said the surface should be hidden. Both were lying to her about the most basic fact of her existence, which is that she is not a surface at all. She is an image of God, a subject with a soul and a will and a mind, made to look out at the world and love it and act in it, precious in God's sight before and beneath and entirely apart from whether anyone ever finds her beautiful. If she believes that, all the way down, the machine loses its grip, because the machine only works on a girl who has agreed to be a surface. And if she does not believe it, no modesty policy in the world will save her, because she will only be a well-covered object instead of an exposed one, still watching herself be watched.

The war for your daughter is not, finally, a war over her clothing. It is a war over whether she is a person or a thing. The world has picked its side. Too often the church, meaning to fight the world, picked the same side in different words. I have five sons and no daughters, and the most useful thing I can do in this war is make sure the men I am sending into it have learned to see a person where the machine trained them to see a thing. That is my part. The daughters are worth every hour of it, and I am not certain we have given them the hours they deserve.

chapters.title: Raising Kids in a Post-Christian Culture
chapters.summary: Your children will not inherit your faith by osmosis. They will inherit it only if it is real enough to survive contact with a world that no longer assumes it is true.
chapters.body:
There is a moment every Christian parent dreads, though few will admit it publicly. It comes at the dinner table, or in the car, or at bedtime — the moment your child looks at you and asks, with genuine confusion, "Why do we believe this when nobody else does?" The question is not hostile. It is honest. And it exposes the central challenge of raising children in a culture that no longer treats Christianity as the default setting of civilized life.

For most of American history, Christian parents operated within a supporting ecosystem. The culture reinforced what parents taught at home. Schools observed Christian holidays. Neighbors went to church. Television programming, for all its flaws, operated within broadly Christian moral assumptions. A child raised in a Christian home in 1975 could go an entire week without encountering a serious challenge to the faith their parents professed. The culture was the water, and Christianity was the current.

That ecosystem has collapsed. The Pew Research Center's 2021 data shows that 29 percent of Americans are religiously unaffiliated — a number that rises to 34 percent among millennials and 36 percent among Gen Z. Your children's friends, by statistical probability, include a significant number who have no religious framework at all. Their teachers may be agnostic. Their coaches may be atheist. The cultural voices they consume on YouTube, TikTok, and podcasts are overwhelmingly secular. Christianity is no longer the current. It is a tributary, and a shrinking one.

This is not a crisis. It may, in fact, be an opportunity. But it demands that Christian parents abandon strategies that worked when the culture did the heavy lifting and develop new ones suited to a world where faith must be chosen rather than assumed.

The first thing to be honest about is the scope of the shift. A Christian child in a public school in 2026 is not merely encountering a few secular ideas. They are immersed in an alternative moral framework — one built on expressive individualism, therapeutic categories of selfhood, and a default skepticism toward institutional religion that is not hostile so much as indifferent. Their classmates are not anti-Christian. They are post-Christian. They have never considered Christianity as a live option, and the few impressions they have of it are likely shaped by culture war headlines and social media caricatures. Your child is not defending the faith against attacks. They are explaining it to people who have never seriously encountered it. That is a fundamentally different challenge, and it requires a fundamentally different preparation.

The Failure of Indoctrination

The instinct of many Christian parents, faced with a hostile or indifferent culture, is to double down on control. Homeschool the children. Restrict their media consumption. Surround them exclusively with Christian friends. Create a hermetically sealed environment in which the faith is never questioned because no alternatives are ever encountered.

The research on this strategy is devastating. The Fuller Youth Institute's "Growing Young" study, led by Kara Powell and Brad Griffin, found that students who had been shielded from doubt and difficult questions in their formative years were more likely — not less — to abandon faith in college. The mechanism is straightforward: a faith that has never been tested is a faith that cannot withstand testing. And testing will come. It always comes.

Christian Smith and Melinda Lundquist Denton, in their landmark National Study of Youth and Religion, found that the dominant religious posture of American teenagers — including those from devoutly Christian homes — was what they called "Moralistic Therapeutic Deism": the vague belief that God exists, wants people to be nice, does not need to be particularly involved in daily life, and exists primarily to make people feel good about themselves. This was not the result of secular indoctrination. It was the result of Christian formation that was a mile wide and an inch deep — that taught rules and stories without forming the intellectual and spiritual muscles needed to hold those stories under pressure.

Indoctrination — the transmission of beliefs without the corresponding development of the capacity to think about those beliefs — produces one of two outcomes. Either the child accepts the beliefs uncritically and becomes a brittle fundamentalist who will shatter at the first serious challenge, or the child rejects the entire framework at the first available opportunity, often with a bitterness proportional to the rigidity of the system they escaped. Neither outcome is faithfulness. Both are failures of formation.

The irony is brutal. The parents who work hardest to protect their children's faith are often the parents most responsible for its eventual destruction. The sealed environment does not produce certainty. It produces a faith that has never developed an immune system — that collapses at the first exposure to a world full of competing ideas, attractive alternatives, and persuasive objections. The child who has been taught that evolution is a lie will not be strengthened when they encounter the evidence in a college biology course. They will be shattered. And the shattering will extend far beyond biology. If the authority figures in their life were wrong about this, the child will reason, what else were they wrong about? The entire edifice comes down, not because the questions are unanswerable but because the child was never given permission to ask them.

Formation Over Information

The alternative to indoctrination is formation — a word that carries different weight. Indoctrination is about content: getting the right beliefs into the child's head. Formation is about character: shaping the kind of person who can hold those beliefs responsibly, question them honestly, and live them out under pressure. The distinction is not merely semantic. It represents two entirely different philosophies of spiritual development.

James K.A. Smith, drawing on Augustine, has argued persuasively that human beings are not primarily thinking things but desiring things. We are not brains on sticks, making rational calculations about which worldview to adopt. We are embodied creatures whose deepest convictions are shaped less by arguments than by practices — by the rhythms of daily life, the stories we inhabit, the communities we belong to, the habits that form us below the level of conscious decision. "Before you think," Smith writes, "you love. Before you love, you are shaped by what you worship."

This means that the most important thing Christian parents do is not the content they teach but the life they model. Children are not persuaded into faith by superior arguments. They are formed into it by the texture of daily life — by watching their parents pray not as performance but as genuine conversation with a God they actually seem to know. By overhearing their parents wrestle with hard questions rather than dismissing them. By experiencing a household where grace is not a theological concept but the actual atmosphere of the home.

Answering "Is God Real?"

When a child asks "Is God real?" the worst possible response is certainty. Not because certainty is always wrong, but because performed certainty — the kind that shuts down the question rather than honoring it — teaches the child that doubt is dangerous, that questions are threats, and that faith means pretending to know things you do not know.

The better response begins with honesty: "I believe God is real, and here is why." The "here is why" matters enormously. If the only reason you can give is "because the Bible says so," you have given your child a circular argument that will not survive their first philosophy class. If the reason is "because I was raised to believe it," you have given them a sociological explanation that applies equally to every religion on earth.

But if you can say, "I believe God is real because I have experienced something in prayer that I cannot explain any other way," or "because the story of Jesus makes sense of the world in ways that no other story does," or "because I have watched people transformed by this faith in ways that I cannot attribute to psychology alone" — then you have given your child something real. Not proof. Real faith has never operated on proof. But testimony — the honest account of one person's encounter with the divine — carries a weight that arguments cannot replicate.

And then add the most important sentence: "But I understand why someone would not believe. There are smart, good, honest people who look at the same evidence and reach a different conclusion. Your faith has to be yours, not mine. I will not love you less if you reach a different answer."

That sentence — "I will not love you less" — is the most evangelistically powerful thing a Christian parent can say. Because the child who knows that their parents' love is not contingent on their belief is the child who is free to believe honestly. And honest belief is the only kind worth having.

Creating Space for Doubt

There is a difference between creating space for doubt and manufacturing it. Creating space for doubt means that when your child says, "I'm not sure I believe in God anymore," you do not panic, lecture, or increase their church attendance. You say, "Tell me more about that." You listen. You take their intellectual development seriously enough to engage with their actual questions rather than the questions you wish they were asking.

Manufacturing doubt, on the other hand, is the error of parents who are so anxious to produce critically thinking children that they introduce challenges before the child has developed the resources to process them. A six-year-old does not need to hear about the Documentary Hypothesis. A ten-year-old does not need a lecture on theodicy. Faith development, like every other form of development, is stage-appropriate. The child psychologist James Fowler mapped six stages of faith development, from the intuitive-projective faith of early childhood through the universalizing faith of mature adulthood. Each stage has its own integrity. Rushing a child through them is as harmful as preventing them from progressing.

The goal is a home where questions are welcome but not weaponized — where a child can express doubt without being shamed and explore alternatives without being abandoned. This requires parents who have done their own intellectual work, who have confronted their own doubts, and who can model the integration of rigorous thinking and genuine faith. Children do not need parents who have all the answers. They need parents who are not afraid of the questions.

Practices That Form

The research on faith transmission is remarkably consistent on one point: practices matter more than programs. The National Study of Youth and Religion found that the single strongest predictor of a young person's faith in adulthood was not youth group attendance, not Christian schooling, not mission trips — but the religious practice of their parents at home. Children whose parents prayed with them, read Scripture with them, and discussed faith openly at home were far more likely to carry that faith into adulthood than children whose parents outsourced formation to the church.

The dinner table is a formative space. Not because parents should turn meals into Bible studies — that is a reliable way to make children dread both dinner and Scripture — but because the table is where a family practices the disciplines of presence, gratitude, and conversation. A simple practice: before the meal, each person names one thing they are grateful for and one thing that was hard about the day. This is not a religious exercise in any formal sense, but it is a deeply formative one. It teaches children to pay attention to their own experience, to name both gift and struggle, and to do so in the presence of people who care. Over years, this practice shapes a posture toward life that is essentially prayerful — attentive, grateful, honest — even before the child has the vocabulary to name it as such.

Bedtime prayers are another formative practice, provided they are not reduced to rote recitation. A child who learns to pray by hearing their parent pray aloud — honestly, in ordinary language, about real things — is learning something no Sunday school curriculum can teach. They are learning that God is someone you talk to, not someone you recite at. They are learning that prayer includes confusion, frustration, and need — not just thanksgiving and request. They are learning that the God their parents worship is big enough to handle the full range of human experience.

Service is formative. Children who grow up watching their parents care for the vulnerable — visiting the sick, feeding the hungry, welcoming the stranger — are receiving a formation in the character of God that no theological lecture can replicate. They are learning that faith is not a set of beliefs to be defended but a way of life to be practiced. And that learning happens below the level of conscious decision, in the realm of habit and desire where the most durable convictions are formed.

Faith vs. Religion

The distinction between passing on faith and passing on religion is the most important distinction a Christian parent can learn to make. Religion, in the sense I mean here, is the external apparatus: the attendance, the vocabulary, the moral code, the tribal identity. Faith is the interior reality: the trust, the relationship, the transformation, the living encounter with the God who is actually there.

It is entirely possible to pass on religion without passing on faith. This is, in fact, the default outcome of most Christian formation in America. The child learns to attend, to perform, to use the right words, to conform to the expected behavior — without ever encountering the living God who is supposed to be at the center of all of it. Christian Smith's research named this precisely: Moralistic Therapeutic Deism is religion without faith. It is the shell without the life.

To pass on faith, you must have faith to pass on. This is the most uncomfortable truth in the entire conversation. If your own faith is merely habitual — if you attend church out of obligation, pray out of superstition, and read Scripture out of guilt — your children will absorb the habit without the substance. They will inherit your religion and discard it as soon as the cultural pressure to maintain it disappears. And that cultural pressure is disappearing rapidly.

But if your faith is alive — if your children see you wrestle with Scripture, weep in prayer, confess failure, extend grace, and return again and again to a God you clearly know and not merely know about — then you are giving them something worth inheriting. Not a set of propositions to be memorized. Not a tribal identity to be maintained. But a relationship to be entered, a life to be lived, a reality to be encountered on their own terms, in their own time, with their own questions.

You cannot control whether your children will believe. That is between them and God, and the sooner you make peace with that, the better parent you will be. What you can control is whether what you hand them is worth believing — whether the faith they see in you is substantial enough, honest enough, and alive enough to survive the world they are growing up in. That is the only question that matters. And it is a question addressed not to your children but to you.

chapters.title: Raising Kids in a Screen and Phone Age
chapters.summary: The phone is not a tool your child uses, it is an environment your child lives inside, and the question is not how to limit it but what kind of person it is training your child to be while you are not looking.
chapters.body:
I want to start by admitting that I am writing this with a phone in my pocket, that I checked it twice while drafting the first paragraph, and that I have lectured my sons about screens with the residual glow of my own screen still in my eyes. Any parent who approaches this subject as a person who has it handled is either lying or has not looked closely. We are all inside this. The device that is forming our children is forming us, and it is forming us first.

So let us throw out the framing we usually start with, the one about screen time, about limits, about how many hours is too many. That framing assumes the phone is a tool, a thing your child picks up, uses for a purpose, and sets down. A hammer is a tool. The phone is not a hammer. The phone is a place. It is an environment with weather and gravity and inhabitants, an environment engineered by some of the most capable people alive to be more compelling than the room your child is physically standing in. When we talk about limiting screen time, we are talking as though we are rationing dessert. We are actually deciding how many hours a day our child lives in a different world than the one we are raising him in.

The research is past arguing about now, and I am not going to pretend it is still an open question. Jonathan Haidt has documented what happened to adolescent mental health beginning around 2012, when the smartphone became universal among teenagers and the front-facing camera turned social life into a permanent performance. The lines on those graphs do not drift. They turn like a hinge, and they turn for girls especially and earliest. Anxiety, depression, self-harm, all rising together at the moment childhood moved onto the screen. Correlation is not proof, and the defenders of the devices have made that point loudly, and it is a fair point as far as it goes. But the defenders have not offered a better account of why an entire generation came apart at precisely the moment its social existence migrated into a machine designed to make it anxious. At some point the burden of proof shifts. I think it has shifted.

Here is what the device is actually doing to a developing soul, underneath the visible behavior. It is teaching your child that he is the center of a feed that exists to serve him, and simultaneously that his worth is set by the reaction of an invisible crowd. Both of those are lies, and they are opposite lies, and the phone tells them at the same time, which is part of why it is so disorienting. The child is sovereign and worthless in the same five minutes. He scrolls a world arranged for his appetite, then posts and waits, heart in his throat, for the verdict of people who do not love him. We did not design a worse machine for forming a self. We could not have if we tried.

And the deeper formation is in what the phone trains attention to do. Attention is not a neutral capacity. It is the thing the whole spiritual life runs on. To pray is to attend. To love a person is to attend to him rather than to yourself. To read scripture, to sit with a hard idea, to be present at a dinner table, all of it is attention, sustained, voluntary, turned outward and held there. The phone is an attention solvent. It dissolves precisely the muscle that faith and love require. A child raised inside it may grow into an adult who literally cannot do the things a deep life is made of, not because he chose against them but because the equipment atrophied before he ever knew he had it.

Consider what the design actually optimizes for, because the people who built these things were not careless and they were not naive. They hired psychologists. They ran experiments on the variable reward schedule, the same mechanism that makes a slot machine impossible to walk away from, the small unpredictable hit of novelty that keeps a hand reaching back to the lever. They built the infinite scroll specifically so there would be no natural stopping point, no bottom of the page where a person might surface and decide he was done. They engineered the notification to interrupt, to fracture the very attention your child needs to learn to hold. None of this is an accident or an unfortunate side effect. It is the product working as intended, because the product is your child's attention and the customer is someone else entirely. When you hand a child a phone you are not handing him a neutral object he will use well or poorly depending on his character. You are seating him at a table where the house always wins and the house has studied him.

There is a grief underneath all of this that I do not want to rush past, because parents feel it and rarely name it. The phone is taking something from the relationship between you and your child that you cannot get back. The hours your teenager spends in his room inside a screen are hours he is not spending with you, and they do not return. The conversations that used to happen in the slow boredom of a car ride now do not happen, because no one is bored anymore, and boredom was the soil a great deal of family conversation grew in. We have eliminated boredom from childhood, and we are discovering that boredom was not the enemy. Boredom was the empty space where a child's own mind woke up and where, sometimes, he turned to the person next to him and said something true.

So what do we actually do. Let me be concrete, because outrage without a plan is just anxiety with a vocabulary.

Delay the smartphone. This is the single most consequential decision available to you, and it gets easier the more parents make it together. The phone that does everything does not belong in the hands of a twelve year old, and the data on early acquisition is grim. A child can have a phone that calls and texts without having a casino, a mall, and a global audience in his pocket. The dumb phone exists. Buy it. You will hear that you are isolating your child, and you must steel-man that, because there is something to it. A child who is the only one without the thing all his friends inhabit pays a social cost, and that cost is real and you should not wave it away. The answer is not to pretend the cost is fake. The answer is to organize with other parents so your child is not the only one, and to accept that some social cost is the price of not handing your eleven year old to an industry that does not love him.

Keep the bedroom clear. No screens behind closed doors at night, no exceptions you would not want to defend in daylight. The phone in the bedroom at night is where most of the damage happens, in the dark, alone, when the defenses are lowest. Charge every device in the kitchen overnight, your own included, because the rule that does not apply to you is not a rule, it is a hypocrisy your children can see straight through.

Watch with them, not just over them. The instinct to police is weaker than the practice of accompanying. Sit with your child and look at what he is looking at, not as an inspector but as a companion. Ask what he thinks. Ask why that video got so many views. Teach him to see the machine that is trying to capture him, because a child who can name the manipulation is partway free of it. The goal is not a child you control. The goal is a child who can eventually control himself, which means a child who understands the thing he is up against.

And build a better room. This is the part we skip, and it is the part that matters most. You cannot subtract the phone and leave a vacuum, because the phone is filling a real hunger, for connection, for stimulation, for a place to be someone. If you take it away and offer nothing, the child will be right to resent you, because you will have made his life worse and called it discipline. So the phone has to be displaced by something with more weight. A family that eats together with the devices in another room. Work that is real, chores that matter, a job that pays. Friends in the physical world, which you will have to engineer because the physical world no longer assembles children automatically the way it once did. A faith practiced visibly in the home. Time outdoors in quantities that feel almost unreasonable. The child raised this way is not deprived. He is given the actual world, which is the thing the screen is a counterfeit of.

I will not pretend any of this is easy, and I will not pretend I have done it cleanly. I have handed a kid a screen to buy myself twenty minutes of quiet, and the twenty minutes was real, and so was the cost. The phone is the path of least resistance for the parent as much as the child. It is the thing that makes the hard hour survivable. Grace covers the days we lose to it. But grace is not a strategy, and the years are short, and the formation is happening whether we direct it or not.

The question was never how much screen time. The question is who our children will be after the machine has had its years with them, and whether we were paying enough attention to notice while it happened. The cruel irony is that paying attention is the one thing the machine is designed to take from us first.

chapters.title: Raising Kids Who Question (Not Kids Who Perform)
chapters.summary: I used to be proud that my children never doubted. I have come to understand that I was proud of the very thing that would eventually break their faith.
chapters.body:
I used to be proud that my children never doubted. They believed what I taught them, cleanly, without argument, and I took this as evidence that I was raising them well, that the faith was taking, that I had transmitted the truth successfully into the next generation. I have come to understand that I was proud of the very thing that would eventually break their faith, because a faith that has never been questioned is not strong. It is untested, and untested faith shatters on first contact with a hard question, and the hard questions always come.

There is a kind of Christian home that produces children who perform belief flawlessly and possess it not at all, and I was building one without knowing it. The child in that home has learned the right answers, the right posture, the right vocabulary, and has learned above all that questions are dangerous, that doubt is failure, that the way to keep the parents' approval and God's is to never let a hard question surface. And so the questions go underground, where they fester, until one day, usually around eighteen or twenty, they erupt, and the performed faith collapses all at once, because it was performance the whole time.

The Faith That Cannot Survive a Question

A faith that cannot survive being questioned is not being protected by our refusal to allow questions. It is being exposed as fragile. When we treat our children's doubts as threats to be shut down, as attacks to be repelled, as evidence of rebellion to be corrected, we teach them that the faith is a delicate thing that cannot bear scrutiny, and children are not stupid, they draw the obvious conclusion, that a belief which cannot be questioned is probably not true.

When you forbid the question, you do not protect the faith. You confirm the child's growing suspicion that the faith would not survive the question. Nothing makes doubt more corrosive than a parent who treats it as forbidden. The forbidding is the confession that we are afraid of the answer.

Contrast this with the God of the Bible, who is remarkably unafraid of questions. Job questions God for chapters, accuses him, demands an answer, and God's response is not to condemn the questioning but to answer it, at length, and then to say that Job spoke rightly, unlike his friends who defended God with tidy pieties. The psalmists question constantly. Thomas doubts and is not cast out but invited to touch the wounds. Jesus fields hostile questions his entire ministry and never once responds by forbidding the question. A God this comfortable with being questioned is not honored by parents who forbid their children to question. He is misrepresented by them.

It is worth sitting with the fact that God answered Job's friends more harshly than he answered Job. The friends did everything a certain kind of Christian parent praises. They defended God, they explained his ways, they refused to entertain the possibility that anything was wrong, they had an answer for every complaint. And God said they had not spoken rightly of him, while Job, who had shaken his fist at heaven and demanded an accounting, had. The honest questioner was closer to God than the confident defenders. If that is how God sorts the wrestlers from the reciters, we should be far more worried about raising reciters than we usually are.

The Difference Between Doubt and Rebellion

We have collapsed two different things into one category and called them both dangerous. Doubt and rebellion are not the same. Rebellion is a turning away from God with the will. Doubt is a wrestling toward God with the mind. And many of the children we accuse of rebellion when they start questioning are not rebelling at all. They are doing the necessary work of making the faith their own instead of merely inheriting it, and they are doing it out loud, in front of us, which is a sign of trust, and we punish the trust as though it were treason.

The child who questions in front of you is honoring you with their honesty. They could hide it. Many do, having learned that questions are unwelcome. The one who brings you the hard question, is the resurrection real, why does God allow suffering, how do we know the Bible is true, why do I have to believe what you believe, is handing you their genuine struggle and asking for help with it. And if we respond with alarm, defensiveness, or discipline, we teach them never to bring us a question again, and the questions do not stop, they just go somewhere we cannot help, which is the worst possible outcome for a parent who wants their child's faith to survive.

I am not pretending the distinction between doubt and rebellion is always clean, because sometimes it is not. Sometimes a child weaponizes doubt, using intellectual questions as a cover for a will that has already decided to do what it wants, and a discerning parent has to be able to tell the difference between a mind that is genuinely wrestling and a heart that is simply looking for permission. But here is what I have learned about telling them apart. You cannot sort the honest questioner from the manipulator by shutting down the questions, because that shuts down both, and drives the honest one into hiding while doing nothing to reach the rebellious one. You can only sort them by welcoming the question, engaging it seriously, and watching what happens. The genuine questioner leans in, wrestles, wants to keep talking. The one using doubt as a cover loses interest the moment the question is actually engaged, because they never wanted an answer, they wanted an exit. Welcome all the questions, and the honest ones will reveal themselves by their hunger, and the manipulative ones by their disinterest, and you will have learned something you could never have learned by forbidding the questions in the first place.

Why Performed Faith Collapses

The tragedy of raising children who perform rather than question is that the performance has an expiration date, and it is usually early adulthood. As long as the child is under our roof and our approval, the performed faith holds, because it is being sustained by our presence and expectations. But the moment they leave, the moment the external scaffolding of the Christian home is removed and they are genuinely free, the performed faith has nothing holding it up, because it was never internalized, it was only enacted, and it falls.

The child who was never allowed to question did not skip the questions. They deferred them. And deferred questions do not weaken with time. They compound. And when they finally come due, all at once, in a dorm room far from home, the faith that could not answer them in childhood cannot answer them now, and it goes.

This is the pattern behind so many stories of young adults abandoning the faith of their childhood. It is often narrated as if the world corrupted them, as if the university stole their faith, as if bad influences pulled them away. Sometimes. But frequently what actually happened is that a performed faith met the first serious question it was never allowed to face, and had no resources, because the resources are built by questioning and this child was never permitted to build them. The world did not take their faith. Their faith was hollow, and the world merely revealed it, and we made it hollow by forbidding the questions that would have made it real.

What Raising a Questioner Requires

Raising a child who questions requires a parent who is not threatened by the question, which requires a parent whose own faith is secure enough to sit with uncertainty. This is the hard part, because our reactions to our children's doubts usually reveal the state of our own. The parent who panics at a child's hard question is often a parent with the same unaddressed question buried in themselves, and the child has poked the wound. If I cannot bear my child's doubt, it is often because I have never made peace with my own.

So the work of raising a questioner begins with the parent's own faith becoming honest. It means being able to say, that is a real question, and I do not have a complete answer, and I have wrestled with it too, and here is what I have found, and here is what I am still not sure about. It means modeling a faith that includes uncertainty rather than pretending to a certainty we do not possess. Children can smell false certainty, and it teaches them that faith requires pretending to know what you do not know, which is a faith they will eventually and rightly reject. A faith honest about its own questions is far more transmissible than a faith that performs certainty it has not earned.

Sitting in the Question With Them

When one of my sons brought me a genuinely hard question, the temptation was always to resolve it quickly, to hand him an answer that would close the question and restore my comfort. I have learned that this is usually the wrong move. Often the more faithful response is to sit in the question with him, to take it seriously, to explore it honestly, to acknowledge its weight, and to resist the urge to prematurely tie it off with an answer that he can tell I reached for out of my own discomfort rather than out of the truth.

Because the goal is not to end the questioning. The goal is to raise a person who can hold hard questions and keep believing, who has learned that faith and questions coexist, who does not experience doubt as the end of faith but as part of its ordinary life. That person is far more durable than the one with all the answers memorized, because when the next question comes, and it will, they will not panic, they will do what they have always done, bring it into the light, wrestle it honestly, and keep walking. That capacity is the thing worth building, and it is built by welcoming questions, not forbidding them.

There is a real discipline in not answering too fast, and it runs against every parental instinct. When your child is troubled by a hard question about God, everything in you wants to relieve the trouble, because you love them and their distress is your distress. But the too-quick answer, even a true one, teaches the child that questions are problems to be eliminated rather than territory to be explored, and it robs them of the muscle they build by staying in the question long enough to find their own footing. Sometimes the most loving thing is to say, that is worth thinking hard about, let us not rush it, and to let the child sit in the discomfort of not-yet-knowing, with you beside them, which is the exact experience they will need to be able to survive when the questions come and you are not there.

The Faith I Actually Want to Leave Them

I came to faith out of atheism, as an adult, through hard questions, not around them. My faith was forged in exactly the kind of relentless questioning I spent years trying to prevent in my own children, which is one of the stranger inconsistencies of my parenting, that I gained my faith by questioning and then tried to give my children a faith that skipped the questioning. My own testimony should have taught me better. The questions did not destroy my atheism's certainties and then leave me with nothing. They carried me, through the wrestling, into a faith that could bear weight precisely because it had been tested.

There is a fear that stops parents from doing this, and I felt it acutely, so I want to name it plainly. The fear is that if you welcome the questions, you might lose the child, that a doubt engaged is a doubt strengthened, that by allowing the questioning you are opening a door the child might walk out of. I understand the fear because I lived inside it for years, and it is exactly backward. The child does not walk out through the door you open by engaging their doubts honestly. The child walks out through the door you slam, the one that tells them their questions are not welcome here, that this faith cannot bear their honesty, that they must choose between their integrity and their belonging. That slammed door is the exit. The open door, the one where a parent says bring me your hardest question and I will not flinch, is not an exit at all. It is the thing that keeps the child in the room, keeps the conversation going, keeps the relationship intact through the very years when so many are lost. You do not lose children by letting them question. You lose them by refusing to.

That is the faith I actually want to leave my sons, not the performed kind that impressed me when they were young, but the wrestled kind that will still be standing when they are fifty and the hard questions have come, as they always come. A faith that has been questioned and survived is not a weaker faith than one that has never been questioned. It is the only strong kind there is. The unquestioned faith is not strong. It is merely untested, and untested is not a virtue, it is a countdown. So I stopped being proud that my children never doubted, and started being grateful when they did, and started welcoming the questions I used to fear, because the questions are not the enemy of their faith. The forbidding of questions is. I forbade them for years. I am trying, now, to be the kind of father a hard question can be brought to, because that father is the one whose children's faith survives him. It is the only inheritance worth leaving, and it cannot be performed. It has to be true, and true things can be questioned, and survive.

chapters.title: Raising Sons
chapters.summary: A father does not disciple his sons mainly through his instructions. He disciples them through his self, and they will absorb who he actually is long before they weigh a word he says.
chapters.body:
I have five sons, and I want to begin by confessing that I am not writing this from the far side of success. My sons are still being formed, and so am I, and some of what I have to say I have learned by getting it wrong first and watching the cost land on people I love. So take this not as a manual from a father who has finished the work, but as field notes from a man still in the middle of it, who has come to a few hard convictions about what actually forms a boy into a good man.

You are the lesson

Here is the first and heaviest conviction. A father does not primarily disciple his sons through what he tells them. He disciples them through who he is. Boys are watching their fathers with a total and mostly unconscious attention, absorbing not the instructions but the man, and what they absorb goes down into a place too deep for later words to reach. You can lecture a boy about honesty for years, but if he watches you shade the truth on the phone he will learn that honesty is what we preach and dishonesty is what we practice, and that second lesson is the one that will stick.

This is a terrifying thing to sit with as a father, because it means the primary curriculum is not my words, over which I have some control, but my character, which my sons observe in its unguarded and unedited state every single day. They see how I treat their mother when I am tired. They see what I do when I am angry, what I reach for when I am anxious, whether I apologize when I am wrong, whether the man in the pulpit and the man in the kitchen are the same man. They are running a continuous and merciless comparison between what I say and what I am, and where the two diverge, they believe the being and discard the saying. I cannot teach my sons to be men I am not willing to be.

Your sons are not mainly listening to your words. They are studying your self, and they will become what they saw, not what they heard.

The power of repentance in front of them

If it is true that our sons absorb who we are, and if it is also true that none of us is who we should be, then it might seem that we are all doomed to hand down our worst selves. But there is a rescue built into fatherhood, and it is one of the most powerful tools a father has, and most of us are too proud to use it. The rescue is repentance performed in front of them.

When a father loses his temper and then goes to his son, specifically, and says, I was wrong to speak to you that way, that was my failure and not yours, I am sorry, will you forgive me, something extraordinary happens in the boy. He does not lose respect for his father, which is the fear that keeps most men from doing it. He gains something far more valuable. He learns that a strong man can be wrong and admit it, that strength and humility are not opposites, that failure is not the end of the story because there is such a thing as repair. And he learns, at a level deeper than any sermon, what grace looks like with skin on it.

The father who never apologizes, who cannot bear to be seen as wrong, teaches his sons that manhood requires the pretense of perfection, and he hands them an impossible and exhausting standard that they will either kill themselves trying to meet or abandon in despair. The father who repents openly hands his sons a manhood they can actually live inside, one that has room for failure because it has room for grace. I have had to go to my sons more times than I would like, to name the specific thing I did and ask them to forgive me, and every time my pride told me it would diminish me in their eyes. It never did. It is the most fathering thing I know how to do.

There is a further gift hidden in this practice, and it is one that shapes a son's entire relationship with God. A son who watches his father repent learns, before he has any theology for it, that failure is survivable, that being wrong is not the end, that there is a way back after you have blown it. This is nearly the whole of the gospel in miniature, learned not from a lesson but from a father's willingness to be humble in front of his child. The son who never sees this grows up believing, at a level too deep to argue with, that he must be good enough, that failure is catastrophic, that there is no way back once you have fallen. And he will bring that belief straight into his life with God, straining to earn an acceptance he could have simply received, all because his father could never model the thing God most wanted him to know.

And there is something a father should understand about the pride that resists this. The refusal to apologize feels, in the moment, like the preservation of a father's authority, as though admitting fault would somehow undermine his standing in the boy's eyes. It is the exact reverse. Authority built on the pretense of never being wrong is brittle, and a growing son sees through it eventually, and when he does, the whole edifice of his father's credibility can collapse at once, because it was built on a lie the boy has now detected. Authority built on honesty, on a father who is strong enough to own his failures, is durable, because it never depended on a perfection the son could see was false. The apologizing father is not the weaker father. He is the one whose authority will still stand when his son is grown and able to see clearly.

The father who apologizes to his son does not lose the boy's respect. He teaches him the one thing no lecture can, that grace is real.

Toughness is not the goal

A great deal of the folk wisdom about raising sons is organized around producing toughness. Do not coddle him, do not let him be soft, teach him not to cry, make him hard enough for the world. I understand the instinct, and the world is genuinely hard and our sons will need real strength to face it. But toughness as the goal is a mistake, and it produces exactly the wounded men we have been describing throughout, the men who can only feel anger, who cannot be close to anyone, who mistake numbness for strength.

When you teach a boy to suppress his tears and deny his fear and lock away everything tender, you are not making him strong. You are making him numb, and numbness is not strength, it is the amputation of half his soul. You are raising the very man who, thirty years later, will sit in my office unable to say why his wife feels alone or why his own children are strangers to him, and the answer will trace back to a father who taught him that a man does not feel. The goal is not a son who feels nothing. The goal is a son who feels everything and knows what to do with it, which is a far higher and harder achievement.

Real strength in a boy is the capacity to feel deeply and to govern what he feels, to be tender without being weak and strong without being hard. That is what we should be forming, and it requires the opposite of the old wisdom. It requires letting our sons feel their feelings in our presence without shame, and then teaching them, patiently, what to do with them, which we can only do if we have learned it ourselves, which most of us have not, which is why this work usually forces a father to grow up alongside his son.

Blessing and the hunger to be seen

There is one more thing a son needs from his father that fathers routinely fail to give, and its absence leaves a hole that a man can spend his whole life trying to fill. A son needs his father's blessing. He needs to hear, in words, plainly and often, that his father is proud of him, that he is loved, that he is enough, that he does not have to earn his place. This is not sentimentality. It is one of the deepest hungers in a boy's soul, the hunger to be seen and delighted in by his father, and it is a hunger that only the father can fill.

The father who withholds this, who assumes his son knows, who thinks affirmation will spoil the boy, who was himself never blessed and so has no template for blessing, raises a son with a permanent ache, a man perpetually trying to earn an approval he never received and can no longer get from the one person whose approval his soul was calibrated to need. So many driven, restless, never satisfied men are simply boys still trying to make a father proud, and often the father is dead, and the approval can never come, and the ache drives them their whole lives.

Letting them see you need God

There is a final thing I want to say to fathers of sons, and it is the one I most often see missed, even by good and serious men. We are careful to let our sons see our strength, our competence, our steadiness, and we are careful, sometimes, to let them see our repentance. But we rarely let them see our dependence, our own need of God, the places where we are not strong and know it and are leaning on grace to get through. And a son who never sees his father's need of God will conclude that faith is for the weak, a thing for people who cannot manage on their own, and that a strong man does not require it.

The most powerful thing a father can show a son about God is not a lecture but the sight of his own father on his knees, genuinely needing the God he is praying to. When a son sees his strong father, the man he most admires, humbly dependent on something greater than himself, he learns that dependence is not weakness, that even the strongest man he knows needs God, and that faith is therefore not a crutch for the incapable but the posture of a real man before his Maker. That single sight, a father who needs God and is not ashamed to show it, does more to commend faith to a son than a thousand arguments.

A son who never sees his father need God will conclude that faith is for the weak. A son who sees his strong father on his knees learns the opposite.

I have found, too, that a son's need to see this grows rather than shrinks as he gets older. The small boy is content to believe his father is invincible, and there may be a season when that belief serves him. But the growing son begins to see the cracks, to notice that his father is not in fact all powerful, and if the father has spent years insisting otherwise, the discovery can be disillusioning, even devastating. If instead the father has let the son gradually see his real dependence on God, then the son's growing awareness of his father's limits is no crisis at all, because he already knew his father leaned on something greater, and he simply learns to lean there too. The honest father prepares his son for the day the illusion of invincibility must fall, by never building the illusion in the first place.

So let your sons see it. Let them see you pray, and not the performed prayer of the confident man but the real prayer of a man who genuinely needs help. Let them see you struggle with something and bring it to God rather than pretending you have it handled. Let them see that the strength they admire in you is itself borrowed, that you are leaning on a strength beyond your own, that the whole edifice of the man they look up to rests on a dependence you are not too proud to admit. That is not a diminishment of your fatherhood. It is the crown of it, because it points them past yourself to the only Father who will never fail them, which is finally the whole point of your fathering.

Speak the blessing. Say the words. Tell your sons plainly and repeatedly that you love them and are proud of them and that their place with you is secure and unearnable. It costs you nothing but the overcoming of your own reticence, and it gives them something they will carry for the rest of their lives. I did not receive this from a father, having grown up without one, and I have had to learn to give what I never got, clumsily and deliberately, saying to my sons the words that no one said to me. It is one of the ways that the grace of God has run backward through my own wound and forward into theirs, and it is, I think, close to the center of what it means to raise a son well.

chapters.title: Single Parenting and the Myth of the Complete Family
chapters.summary: The church built a myth of the complete family and then quietly told single parents they had failed to build it. But the God who raised his own people had no such family either.
chapters.body:
I was raised without a father. That fact is not a footnote in my life. It is closer to the center of it, and it shapes how I read every Christian conversation about the family, especially the ones conducted by people who have never known its absence. Because the church I eventually joined had a great deal to say about the family, and much of it, however unintentionally, landed on a boy like me as an indictment. Your family was incomplete. Something was missing. The implied conclusion, never quite spoken but always felt, was that I was missing something too.

I want to write toward the single parents, and toward the children of single parents, and toward a church that has too often handed both a burden dressed up as a doctrine. And I want to do it honestly, which means naming the ways the church built a myth of the complete family and then quietly taxed the people who did not fit it.

The myth we mistook for the gospel

Somewhere along the way, a particular arrangement of the family, two parents, a mother and a father, children between them, became elevated in the Christian imagination to the status of a near-sacrament. The nuclear family became the assumed default of every sermon, every ministry, every program. And whatever does not fit that shape came to be seen, however gently, as broken, deficient, a deviation from the design.

But this elevation of the nuclear family is not as biblical as we assume. It owes at least as much to a particular era of Western culture as it does to Scripture. The families of the Bible are a chaotic assortment of arrangements, blended and extended and irregular, held together by covenant more than by tidy structure. The people of God were formed not around the nuclear family but around a covenant community that repeatedly extended itself to the widow, the orphan, the stranger, precisely those whom the nuclear-family ideal leaves out. When we made the intact nuclear family the standard, we quietly abandoned the very people Scripture instructs us to gather in.

The church took a cultural arrangement and baptized it as the divine design, then handed the bill to everyone whose family did not fit the frame. That is not the gospel. That is a preference wearing the gospel's clothing.

The isolated nuclear household, mother and father and children alone in a single dwelling, self-sufficient and turned inward, is a relatively recent development in human history, and a peculiarly modern one at that. For most of human existence, families were embedded in extended networks of kin and community, and children were raised by many hands. When the church made the modern nuclear family the measure of a real family, it did not recover a biblical ideal. It absorbed a cultural accident and gave it the authority of divine command.

What the myth does to a child

I know what the myth does to a child, because it did it to me. When the entire architecture of your church assumes a father in the home, a boy without one absorbs the message that his family is a problem, that his situation is a deficiency, that he is starting the race behind. No one has to say it. The assumption says it. Every Father's Day sermon that celebrated the family I did not have said it. Every ministry built around a structure my family lacked said it.

And the deeper wound was theological. When I was told that God was a father, the metaphor that was meant to comfort me instead named my wound. The very language the church used to describe God's love was borrowed from the relationship I had been denied. It took me years to understand that God being a father was not an insult to my fatherlessness but its answer, that the God who describes himself as father to the fatherless was speaking directly to a boy like me, offering not a reminder of absence but the promise of a presence that would not leave. But no one framed it that way. The church assumed the earthly father and lost the boy who did not have one.

To the single parent carrying it alone

If you are a single parent, I want to say something to you that the church has not said often enough. You are not a broken version of a real family. You are a family. Complete, whole, sufficient, held by the God who has always specialized in the family the world calls incomplete. The exhaustion you carry, the double load of being both provider and nurturer, of making every decision without a partner to share the weight, of falling into bed at night with no one to say you did well today, that exhaustion is holy, and it is seen, even when no one around you seems to see it.

The myth of the complete family did not just wound your children. It wounded you, by teaching you to see your own faithful, sacrificial, exhausting love as somehow second-rate. It is not second-rate. The love you pour out, alone, into your children, is as full and as real and as blessed as any love poured out by two. God does not grade families on a curve of structure. God looks at the love, and your love, single parent, is not diminished by the fact that you carry it alone. If anything, it is magnified by the weight you bear to give it.

Your family is not missing a piece. It is a whole thing, held by a whole God, and the love you give alone is not worth less than the love others give together. The scale God uses does not measure structure. It measures love.

I watched my own mother carry this weight, and I did not understand, as a boy, what it cost her. I understand better now. The single parent lives without the thing every married parent takes for granted, a second set of hands, a second perspective, someone to trade off with when the well runs dry. There is no trading off when you parent alone. The well runs dry and you keep drawing from it anyway, because there is no one else to draw. That is not a lesser love. That is a love that has been tested in a fire most parents never have to enter.

The community that was supposed to be there

Here is where the church must repent, and where I include myself in the repentance, because I have led churches that did this. When Scripture speaks of the fatherless and the widow, it does not merely offer them a metaphor of divine care. It commands the community to become the answer. The people of God are supposed to be the extended family that surrounds the single parent, that provides the men to mentor the fatherless boy and the women to come alongside the exhausted mother, that fills in what a single parent cannot provide alone, not out of pity but out of covenant.

We have largely failed at this. We built programs for the intact families and left the single parents to fend for themselves, and then we had the audacity to lament the state of the fatherless generation, as though the community bore no responsibility for the fathering it was commanded to provide. If the church took seriously its calling to be the family of the fatherless, single parenting would not carry the isolation it carries. The single parent was never meant to parent alone. The community was supposed to show up. The failure of the child is often, at bottom, the failure of a church that would not become the family it was told to be.

The father to the fatherless

Let me speak now to the deepest wound, the one I carry myself. To the child raised without a father, or a mother, there is a specific ache that never fully resolves, a hunger for a presence that was not there. I will not pretend the gospel makes that ache disappear. It does not. I still feel it, decades later, in moments I do not expect. But I have come to know something about that ache that changed my relationship to it.

The God who calls himself a father to the fatherless is not offering a metaphor to paper over the wound. He is offering himself as the presence I was denied. Not a replacement that erases the loss, but a companion who enters the loss and refuses to leave. The fatherlessness was real. The presence of God in the fatherlessness was also real. And I have found, over the long years, that the very wound of my father's absence became the place where I learned most deeply what it means to be fathered by God, because I had nowhere else to put the hunger.

I do not say this to romanticize the wound or to suggest that the absence was somehow good. It was not good. A boy should have a father, and the God who calls himself father to the fatherless would be the first to say so, because the very naming of the wound as something God must answer is an admission that the wound should not have been there. But I have learned that God does not waste our wounds. The hunger my father's absence carved into me became a capacity for God, a place already hollowed out and waiting to be filled, and the God who filled it did not fill it in spite of the absence but by way of it. This is the strange grace at the heart of the gospel, that God enters our worst losses not to explain them away but to be present in them, and that the very places where we were most abandoned can become the places where we are most deeply found.

The temptation to overcompensate

There is a trap that waits for the single parent who has absorbed the myth of the incomplete family, and it is the trap of overcompensation. Believing their child is starting behind, the single parent tries to be both parents at once, to fill every role, to make up by sheer effort for the absence the myth has told them is a deficit. And the effort, however loving, can become its own burden, both for the parent who cannot sustain it and for the child who feels the weight of being someone their parent must heroically compensate for.

You do not have to be two parents. You cannot be, and the attempt to be will exhaust you and communicate to your child that they are a problem being managed rather than a person being loved. What your child needs is not two parents worth of effort from one exhausted person. What they need is one parent who is present, who is at peace, who is not frantically trying to prove that the family is not lacking. A single parent who has made peace with their situation, who is not driven by the shame of the myth, offers their child something far more stabilizing than a parent scrambling to be everything. Let the community be the other hands. Let God be the father to the fatherless. Your job is to be the one parent you are, fully and without shame, and to trust that the rest is held by hands larger than yours.

I have watched single parents pour themselves out until there was nothing left, driven by the fear that any moment of rest, any admission of need, any acknowledgment of their own limits, would confirm the verdict the world had already handed down. This is a cruelty the myth imposes, and it must be resisted, because a depleted parent cannot love well, and a parent who models a life of grinding self-erasure teaches their children that love means the annihilation of the self. It does not. Even God rested. The single parent who guards a measure of rest, who receives help without shame, who tends their own soul as well as their children's, is not failing. They are modeling a sustainable love, a love that can go the distance precisely because it does not pretend to be infinite. Your children do not need a martyr. They need a parent who is still standing years from now, and the way to still be standing is to refuse the myth's demand that you empty yourself completely.

What I want the single parent to hear

You are not raising broken children in a broken family. You are raising loved children in a family God calls whole. The world's myth of completeness is not the gospel's measure. The gospel measures love, and covenant, and faithfulness, and by every one of those measures your family stands complete before God, whatever it lacks by the world's arithmetic.

And to the church, I say we have a debt to pay. We owe the single parents among us the community we were commanded to provide. We owe the fatherless the fathering the covenant obligates us to supply. We owe every family that does not fit the myth an unlearning of the myth, and a return to the God whose own people were never a tidy nuclear arrangement but a gathered community of the broken, the widowed, the orphaned, and the alone, made whole not by their structure but by the God who dwelt among them. That God dwells among the single-parent family too, and calls it not incomplete, but his own.

chapters.title: Sports, Activities, and the Idol of the Well-Rounded Child
chapters.summary: I once drove ninety minutes each way, four nights a week, to a sport my son did not love, for a college scholarship that did not exist, and I called it good parenting.
chapters.body:
I once drove ninety minutes each way, four nights a week, to a sport my son did not particularly love, for a college scholarship that did not exist, and I called it good parenting. We ate dinner in the car. We did not eat it together at a table, as a family, more than a couple nights a week, for years. And if you had asked me why, I would have told you I was investing in my son, giving him opportunities, raising a well-rounded child. I was doing something. I am no longer sure it was good, and I am fairly sure it was worship, just not of God.

The well-rounded child is one of the most respectable idols in the modern Christian home, and it is an idol precisely because it is respectable. No one questions it. Everyone is doing it. The whole culture affirms it. Which is exactly the condition under which an idol operates best, when the sacrifice it demands is so normal that no one thinks to ask whether the god is worth it.

The Cult of Enrichment

Somewhere in the last few decades, parenting mutated into a competitive project of maximizing a child's development, and the currency of that project became activities. Sports, and travel sports, and multiple sports, plus music, plus tutoring, plus clubs, plus the strategic accumulation of experiences designed to produce a well-rounded, high-achieving, competitive young person. The child's calendar filled up. The family's calendar filled up. And the filling was experienced not as a problem but as diligence, as the very evidence that you were a devoted parent.

We measure our devotion as parents by how full our children's schedules are, and then we wonder why our families feel frantic and disconnected. The fullness is not a side effect of the frenzy. It is the frenzy. We chose it, and we called it love.

Notice what the cult of enrichment displaces. It displaces the family dinner, which every serious study says is one of the most protective things in a child's life and which is impossible when three children have three activities in three directions at 6 p.m. It displaces unstructured time, in which children learn to be bored and then learn to be creative. It displaces the Sabbath, which we skip constantly for tournaments while telling ourselves God understands. It displaces rest, presence, and the slow ordinary time in which relationships are actually built. We traded all of that for enrichment, and we did not even notice we were trading, because everyone around us was making the same trade.

What the Idol Promises

Every idol makes a promise, and this one's promise is safety through achievement. If I fill my child with enough activities, develop enough of their potential, position them well enough, then they will succeed, and success will keep them safe, and their safety will justify my anxiety. The travel team is really a sacrifice offered to secure a future. The packed schedule is a hedge against the terrifying possibility that my child might fall behind, might not get in, might not measure up, might not be okay.

And underneath that, if we are honest, is often the parent's own need. The child's achievement becomes the parent's report card. The trophy on the shelf is the parent's trophy. I have sat in the stands and felt my own worth rise and fall with my son's performance, and that is a diagnostic. When my emotional state depends on how my child does at a game, the game has stopped being for the child and started being for me. The child has become the instrument of the parent's identity, which is precisely the dynamic Scripture calls idolatry, we have just moved it from a golden statue to a soccer field.

There is a particular ugliness in how this reveals itself in the stands, and I have been part of it, so I am not describing other people. The way a parent's voice changes when their child underperforms. The car ride home that becomes a coaching session the child did not ask for. The disappointment, barely hidden, that the child reads instantly and absorbs as a verdict on their worth. The child learns, from a thousand small signals, that dad is happier when I perform well, that my failures cost him something, that the love in the house rises and falls with the scoreboard. No parent means to teach this. Every parent who has staked their identity on their child's achievement teaches it anyway, in the car, on the drive home, in the tone.

What It Costs the Child

Here is the cruelest part. We tell ourselves the enrichment is for the child, but the child often pays the highest price. The overscheduled child does not experience their packed life as enrichment. They experience it as pressure, as a treadmill, as a series of performances they cannot stop performing because the family has organized itself around them. Anxiety in children has risen alongside the enrichment culture, and I do not think that is a coincidence. We have raised a generation of children who cannot rest because they were never taught how, whose worth got attached to output before they could read.

A child who is only ever busy learns that they are only valuable when producing. That belief does not stay in childhood. It becomes an adult who cannot rest, cannot sit still, cannot believe they are loved apart from what they achieve. We install that in the minivan, one tournament at a time.

And the well-rounded child, ironically, is often a child who is not deeply anything. Spread across a dozen activities, they never sink into the depth that comes from sustained attention to one thing loved for its own sake. Breadth is not the same as depth, and a life of managed breadth can produce a person who is competent at everything and passionate about nothing, who does things to build a résumé rather than because they love them, who has never learned the difference. We aimed at well-rounded and we sometimes hit hollow.

The Sabbath We Keep Sacrificing

Let me name the specifically theological failure, because it is where the idol shows its face most clearly. God built rest into the structure of creation and into the Ten Commandments, ranked alongside do not murder and do not steal. Remember the Sabbath, keep it holy. And we break it, weekly, without a flicker of conscience, for youth sports. The tournament is on Sunday. The practice runs through dinner. The season swallows the season of rest God commanded.

We would never let our children skip a commandment about honesty or stealing for a soccer tournament, but we let them, and ourselves, skip the one about rest without a second thought, because the idol of achievement has taught us that rest is optional and productivity is mandatory. That is exactly backward. God did not make rest optional. He made it a command and a gift and a weekly declaration that the world does not depend on our striving. When we sacrifice it for enrichment, we teach our children that their striving is more sacred than God's rhythm. They learn the lesson. It shapes their entire relationship with work and worth for the rest of their lives.

Consider what the Sabbath was originally for, because it clarifies exactly what we are trading away. God gave the Sabbath to a people who had just come out of slavery, out of Egypt, where they had been worked without rest, where their worth was measured entirely in bricks produced, where a human being was only as valuable as their output. And the first thing God did with a free people was command them to stop, one day in seven, to prove to themselves that they were no longer slaves, that their value did not depend on their production, that the world would keep turning while they rested. The Sabbath is a weekly declaration of freedom from the tyranny of achievement. And here we are, generations later, voluntarily marching our children back into Egypt, filling every seventh day with more production, teaching them that their worth is in their output after all, that stopping is falling behind, that a human being is only as valuable as their performance. We escaped Pharaoh and rebuilt his brickyard in our own minivans, and we hung a trophy over it, and called the whole thing love.

The Question I Should Have Asked

The question I never asked, in all those years of driving ninety minutes each way, was simple. What is this for. Not what am I hoping it produces, but what is it actually for, right now, in the life of my family and the soul of my son. If the honest answer is that it is building my child's résumé, feeding my anxiety, and displacing the family and the Sabbath and the rest, then I should have the courage to call it what it is and stop, or at least to prune it back to something a family can survive.

There is nothing wrong with a sport a child loves, an instrument that brings them joy, an activity that genuinely enriches. The problem is not activity. The problem is the idol, the belief that more is always better, that a full schedule is devotion, that a child's worth and safety are secured through achievement, and that the family should organize itself around the maximization of the children's potential at the cost of everything else. That belief is a lie, and it is an expensive one, and the bill comes due in anxious children and frantic families and a Sabbath none of us keep.

Pruning is harder than it sounds, because the enrichment culture punishes the family that opts out. The child who does not play travel ball at eight cannot make the team at twelve, because the system has front-loaded the commitment, deliberately, to capture families early and hold them through fear of falling behind. So the decision to prune is not costless. Your child may genuinely miss opportunities other children get. You have to decide whether those opportunities are worth what they cost, and the honest answer, most of the time, once you actually count the cost in dinners and Sabbaths and presence, is that they are not. But you will have to make that decision alone, against the current, while every other family in the stands makes the opposite one, and calls it love.

What I Would Do Differently

I would let my children be less busy and more present. I would protect the family dinner as though it mattered, because it does. I would let a season go by where a son did nothing organized at all and learned to fill his own time. I would keep the Sabbath even when the tournament was scheduled, and let my child miss the tournament, and let that be a lesson more valuable than any trophy, that our family bows to God's rhythm and not to the calendar of youth sports. I would ask, of every activity, what is this for, and I would be willing to hear an answer I did not like.

And I would try, above all, to disentangle my own worth from my children's performance, because that is the root the whole idol grows from. As long as my identity rose and fell with my son's game, I was going to keep sacrificing the family on the altar of his achievement, no matter how many articles like this one I read or wrote. The idol does not die because you criticize it. It dies when you stop needing what it promises, when you find your worth somewhere it cannot be threatened by a missed goal or a benched season or a scholarship that goes to another kid. For the Christian, that somewhere is supposed to be the love of God, which does not fluctuate with anyone's performance, mine or my child's. I say supposed to be because I have preached that love for years and still caught myself dying a little in the stands when my son struck out, which tells me the idol had a deeper hold on me than my theology did. Killing it is not a matter of driving less. It is a matter of believing, all the way down, that I am already loved, and that my children are already loved, entirely apart from what any of us produce. When that belief goes deep enough, the frantic schedule loses its grip on its own, because there is nothing left for it to promise.

I am not sure my sons needed to be well-rounded. I am sure they needed a father who was present, a family that ate together, a rest they were allowed to take, and a sense that they were loved entirely apart from anything they achieved. The idol of the well-rounded child promised me that if I filled their lives, I would secure their future. What it actually delivered was a lot of dinners in the car and a season of my sons' childhood spent in transit toward scholarships that did not exist. I would trade all of it back for the years at the table. That table was the enrichment. I just could not see it, because everyone around me was driving somewhere too, and we all called it love.

chapters.title: Teaching Kids to Pray (Not Perform)
chapters.summary: The first prayer my son ever prayed out loud was a lie, and I taught it to him. Not on purpose. But I taught it just the same.
chapters.body:
The first prayer my son ever prayed out loud was a lie, and I taught it to him. Not on purpose. But I taught it just the same. He was four, sitting at the dinner table, and I asked him to thank God for the food. He folded his hands the way he had seen me fold mine, closed his eyes the way he had seen me close mine, and said the words he had heard a hundred times: "Thank you God for this food and this day and my family, amen." Perfect. Fluent. And empty. He was not talking to God. He was performing a shape he had learned from watching me, and I applauded, because the shape was correct.

I want to be careful not to make this sound worse than it was. He was four. Four-year-olds imitate everything, and imitation is how children learn most of what they know, including how to speak to God, so there was nothing sinister in the moment itself. The problem was not that he imitated. The problem was what he was imitating, and the fact that I could not tell the difference between a child learning to pray and a child learning to sound like he was praying, because I had long since lost the ability to tell that difference in myself.

I did not notice for years what I had done. I thought I was teaching him to pray. I was teaching him to sound like someone who prays. Those are not the same skill, and the second one is easier to teach, easier to measure, and quietly poisonous.

The Prayer That Impresses the Room
